title: The STEM Admissions Counselor Helping Students Stand Out at Stanford, Yale, Berkeley & More
excerpt: Samuel Ortiz has advised students who have gone on to attend highly selective universities, including Stanford , the University of California, Berkeley , Yale , Columbia , Duke , Johns Hopki…

author.name: Samuel Ortiz
author.bio: Samuel Ortiz is a former university professor and senior STEM admissions consultant at Blue Stars, mentoring students to admissions at Stanford, Yale, and UC Berkeley.

contentHtml:
Samuel Ortiz has advised students who have gone on to attend highly selective universities, including Stanford, the University of California, Berkeley, Yale, Columbia, Duke, Johns Hopkins, Northwestern, and Rice, among others. This past year alone, two of his students were admitted to Stanford. His students pursued fields including Symbolic Systems, Computer Science, Data Science, Applied and Computational Mathematical Sciences, Electrical Engineering, Computer Engineering, Biomedical Engineering, and Astrophysics.

Drawing on his experience as a college admissions counselor and former professor of English, Samuel helps students identify their intellectual interests, experiences, and values, then translate those strengths into a compelling profile, application, and essays. From sourcing meaningful extracurricular and academic opportunities to shaping a distinctive personal narrative, he supports students at every stage of their journey, from early exploration in the underclass years to the final stages of the application process. Over the course of his career, he has worked with hundreds of students from a wide range of geographic, cultural, and personal backgrounds. His approach emphasizes thoughtful positioning, authentic self-reflection, and a nuanced understanding of how admissions officers evaluate applications in context.

Samuel holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in English. In addition to his counseling work, he has volunteered as an organizer for college admissions fairs serving first-generation and historically underrepresented students, reflecting his personal commitment to expanding educational opportunity and helping students navigate unfamiliar systems with confidence.

Outside of counseling, Samuel enjoys reading, writing, and creating unique music playlists while spending time with his two cats, Nugget and Noodles.

DrM: Two of your students were admitted to Stanford in 2026. What’s your secret to helping students achieve such success?

Samuel: Most important is helping students discover what genuinely makes them unique.

That starts with getting to know them—their interests, values, and the kinds of problems they’re naturally drawn to. From there, I help them pursue opportunities that align with those interests. When students are genuinely excited about something, they’re more likely to excel, and that authenticity comes through in their application.

For example, one of the students admitted to Stanford this past year had longstanding interests in AI, neuroscience, and music. At first, she worried that her interests were too wide-ranging to fit together into a compelling application. However, after reading about an AI and music project, she reached out to the researcher herself and eventually joined the lab. She spent the next year exploring this unique intersection, and by the time she applied to college, her essays reflected years of genuine, highly distinctive intellectual exploration rather than a collection of activities assembled to impress an admissions office.

My years of guiding hundreds of students through the admissions process and studying successful applications helps me uncover the motivations, values, and experiences that allow students to present the strongest, most distinctive version of themselves.

DrM: You’ve also worked with students admitted to UC Berkeley, Yale, Columbia, Duke, Johns Hopkins, Northwestern, and Rice, among others. What do you think distinguishes your approach to guiding students to stand out in such competitive pools?

Samuel: My approach is very collaborative. I listen closely to student feedback, adapt to the individual, and help each student build a path that feels authentic to who they are. I see my role as part strategist, part teacher, and part mentor: I simplify an overwhelming process, help students clarify their interests, and guide them toward experiences that reveal their values.

For example, one of my students who was accepted to UC Berkeley’s highly competitive computer science program felt overwhelmed by the constant stream of admissions advice online and worried she wasn’t doing enough. Rather than encouraging this student to chase every new trend, I focused on identifying the common thread throughout her many extracurriculars. Whether she was recruiting girls into AP Computer Science, designing engaging STEM lessons for elementary students, teaching programming at a homeless shelter, or conducting data science research, the same motivation kept appearing: making tech accessible. Once we identified that theme, we built her application around it. By helping her tune out the noise and build an admissions profile around her authentic interests, she gained entrance to her dream school.

Storytelling is also central to everything I do. I don’t see storytelling as inventing a narrative. A good narrative, like good research, depends on evidence. I help students look at their choices, projects, challenges, and interests, then understand what those experiences reveal about who they are and what they will contribute to a university community.

DrM: Top engineering programs see thousands of applicants with strong math and science grades. What separates the students who get in from the ones who don’t?

Samuel: Strong grades in advanced math and science are important, but at the most competitive engineering programs, they’re expected.

What often separates students is what they do with that knowledge outside the classroom––through independent research, competitions, or practical applications, like internships. Top schools also want to see leadership so they can understand who this person is outside of their high school accomplishments. For instance, another student who ultimately enrolled at UC Berkeley discovered her passion for biology in the classroom, but she didn’t stop there. She pursued cancer research through a fellowship at UC Irvine, where she investigated carcinogenic cellular processes and discovered a love for biomolecular research. That willingness to apply what she learned at an advanced level became one of the defining strengths of her application.

I also encourage students to explore unexpected intersections. Some students combine computer science with art, music, or the humanities. Others become deeply immersed in a very specific area of research. Those paths may look different, but they both demonstrate intellectual curiosity and a genuine desire to explore ideas beyond what’s required in school.

Knowledge matters, but curiosity, initiative, and long term commitment are often what make a student stand out.

DrM: Many strong STEM students are excellent at the technical work but struggle to write compellingly about it. How do you help a student translate technical projects or research into an essay that actually engages an admissions reader?

Samuel: When it comes to application essay writing, many STEM students know their projects inside and out, but they naturally focus on the technical details. The challenge is that technical details alone don’t tell an admissions reader much about the student.

My process usually starts with conversation rather than writing. I’ll ask students why they chose the project, what excites them about it, what challenges they encountered, and what bigger questions they hope to answer or problems they hope to solve. As we talk, we begin uncovering the “why” behind the work. For the UC Berkeley CS student excited about tech accessibility, that meant realizing that an after-school coding program wasn’t simply about learning to code; rather, it reflected a desire to create more opportunities for women in STEM.

Once we understand that motivation and larger purpose, the essay becomes much easier to write. The technical project is still an important part of the story, but it’s no longer the whole story. The student’s curiosity, values, and reasons for pursuing the work become just as important as the work itself.

DrM: How early should a family start thinking about engineering admissions strategy — and what does that look like for a 9th or 10th grader who’s still exploring?

Samuel: For competitive engineering programs, the earlier students begin exploring, the better. Top colleges look for long-term, sustained involvement in the particular areas of STEM that excite students. At many highly competitive high schools, it’s not uncommon for the strongest engineering applicants to complete advanced coursework like AP Calculus BC well before senior year: it opens the door to higher-level math, college coursework, research opportunities, and more advanced engineering experiences. Those opportunities, in turn, give students more chances to discover what genuinely excites them and to develop meaningful expertise over time.

More importantly, discovering genuine interest takes time. You can’t rush curiosity, and you can’t cram meaningful experiences into the months before applications are due. One’s high school years go by faster than you’d think!

DrM: What do you hope students take away from working with you, beyond the acceptance letter itself?

Samuel: I hope students leave the process with greater confidence and peace of mind.

College admissions can be incredibly stressful, and I believe students benefit from having someone who can simplify the process, provide encouragement, and help them focus on what truly matters.

I also hope students leave with stronger critical thinking skills and a better understanding of themselves. The admissions process requires a great deal of reflection, and my goal is to help students develop the ability to think deeply about both their own experiences and the world around them.

Ultimately, I want students to feel that they were genuinely mentored, not just guided through an application, but encouraged to pursue the interests and opportunities that matter most to them.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
What the CS Job Crisis Means for Your Child’s Future

Not long ago, a CS degree from Stanford was about as close to a guaranteed outcome as higher education offered. Tech companies recruited aggressively on campus. Signing bonuses were generous. Entry-level offers from Google, Meta, and Apple came easily. That era appears to be over, at least for now. The CS job crisis and the rapid evolution of future STEM careers are forcing families to rethink how students prepare for the modern economy.

Stanford associate professor Jan Liphardt recently told the Los Angeles Times that graduates “are struggling to find entry-level jobs” at major tech companies. He considers it “a dramatic reversal from three years ago, when all of my undergraduate mentees found great jobs at the companies around us.”

The data backs him up. Employment among software developers aged 22–25 has fallen roughly 20% from its late-2022 peak, according to a Stanford Digital Economy Lab analysis of ADP payroll data. A Stanford study also found that entry-level hiring for AI-exposed jobs — roles for which AI can perform or assist with a significant share of the tasks involved, making human hires easier to reduce — declined 13% relative to less-exposed roles. Unemployment for CS graduates has climbed to around 6%, a level that would have seemed unthinkable just a few years ago.

The shake-up isn’t limited to Stanford. Students at UC Berkeley, USC, and schools across California are feeling it too, and the picture is even starker for graduates of less elite programs.

What’s Driving the CS Job Crisis?

The easy narrative is: AI is taking CS jobs. The truth is more nuanced — and in some ways more important for families planning a college strategy.

AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot have genuinely changed how software gets built. Managers who once staffed projects with ten junior developers can now achieve comparable output with two senior engineers and an AI assistant. That structural shift has hit entry-level roles hardest, because junior coders were traditionally doing exactly the kind of routine, repetitive programming that AI handles well.

But there’s also a macro-economic component. During the post-2020 zero-interest-rate period, tech companies went on massive hiring binges. Meta, for example, grew from roughly 45,000 to over 86,000 employees in three years. When the Fed raised rates aggressively starting in 2022, those same companies overcorrected, laying off tens of thousands and raising the bar for every new hire. New graduates entering that tightened market found themselves competing against experienced engineers who’d been let go.

The result: a bifurcated job market where a small slice of graduates — those with deep AI skills, thick project portfolios, and real-world research experience — are landing good jobs, while everyone else is scrambling. Many Stanford students are now opting for a fifth-year master’s program just to delay their job search and add credentials. As one graduate put it, “Half of my friends are still on campus doing their fifth-year master’s.”

What This Means for High School College Planning

For families, the real takeaway is this: general software programming is a surprisingly small corner of STEM, and it happens to be the corner AI is disrupting most. The rest of STEM tells a very different story. Fields like biomedical engineering, data science, robotics, and cybersecurity are projected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics to grow nearly three times faster than non-STEM roles through 2034. The question isn’t whether to pursue STEM. It’s which STEM path, and how to pursue it strategically.

Here’s what the data and current market conditions suggest are the strongest options for today’s high schoolers.

AI-Resilient STEM and Tech Paths Worth Pursuing

1. AI/ML Engineering & Research: The demand for people who can build and advance AI systems, not just use them, remains extremely strong. AI professionals earn between $96,000 and $200,000 per year, and some analysts project job growth of 26% over the coming decade. This is the field that’s reshaping every other field. Students who want to go deep into CS should specialize here rather than pursuing general software engineering.

2. Cybersecurity: As AI-powered threats grow more sophisticated, so does the need for defenders. Cybersecurity is a national security priority, and the U.S. faces a significant shortage of skilled professionals in this area. Roles span risk assessment, security architecture, threat intelligence, and policy — giving students with varying strengths a range of entry points. The field is highly resistant to automation precisely because it requires adversarial, creative thinking that AI tools struggle to replicate.

3. Data Science & Business Intelligence: Data scientists and analysts sit at the intersection of technical skill and human judgment. AI can generate insights; humans still have to interpret them, communicate them to stakeholders, and make consequential decisions based on them. The market research and analytics field is projected to grow 34% over the next decade, with top earners exceeding $194,000 annually.

4. Robotics & Embedded Systems Engineering: Robotics is one of the most AI-resistant corners of the tech world, precisely because it requires making AI work in messy, unpredictable physical environments. The field is growing 9–13% annually. Top programs are at Carnegie Mellon, MIT, Georgia Tech, and Michigan. Students who like the intersection of hardware and software, building things that interact with the real world, are well suited here.

5. Electrical & Computer Engineering (with AI Specialization): Traditional electrical engineering such as  power systems, control systems, semiconductor design remains deeply valuable and relatively insulated from the current AI disruption. Pairing an ECE foundation with machine learning coursework positions students for roles in chip design, autonomous systems, and industrial automation that are difficult to automate away.

6. Biomedical Engineering & Health Tech: The combination of an aging population, a growing healthcare system, and the rapid deployment of AI in medicine creates enormous demand for engineers who understand both biology and technology. Nursing holds the lowest unemployment rate of any degree at 2.1%, and biomedical fields adjacent to healthcare show similarly strong job security.

7. Bioinformatics & Computational Biology: One of the fastest-growing and most underappreciated intersections in all of STEM. Bioinformatics combines biology, statistics, and programming to analyze genomic data, model disease, and accelerate drug discovery — and it is specifically highlighted in the Stanford 2026 AI Index as a resilient growth area. Students with interests in both life sciences and data are unusually well positioned here. This is one of the few fields where being a skilled programmer and a skilled biologist is genuinely additive rather than redundant.

8. Quantum Computing: Still early-stage, but attracting enormous investment from Google, IBM, Microsoft, and the federal government. The talent pipeline is almost empty at the entry level, meaning students who build quantum literacy now will face far less competition than in any other emerging field. Students pursuing physics or applied math who develop quantum literacy will be poised for roles that will be in extremely high demand within the decade.

9. Nuclear Engineering: A field experiencing a genuine renaissance. With major tech companies like Google and Microsoft signing contracts for nuclear energy to power their data centers, and the federal government investing heavily in next-generation reactor design, nuclear engineers are in high demand for the first time in a generation. It’s one of the most durable and physically irreplaceable engineering disciplines.

10. Environmental & Civil Engineering: Infrastructure is having a moment. Federal investment in roads, bridges, power grids, and water systems is driving sustained demand for civil engineers (projected 7–8% growth), who work on projects that are inherently local, physical, and resistant to remote or AI-driven displacement. Environmental engineering adds the additional tailwind of clean energy transition and climate adaptation work.

11. Supply Chain & Operations Engineering (Industrial Engineering): Underappreciated and highly employable. Industrial and systems engineers who specialize in supply chain optimization and operations are in strong demand at companies like Amazon, Apple, and major manufacturers, with work that is AI-augmented rather than AI-displaced. These roles require the kind of systems thinking and process judgment that AI tools currently support but cannot replace.

12. AI Ethics, Governance & Policy: Best pursued as a combined or double major rather than a standalone — think CS + Philosophy, Data Science + Public Policy, or Computer Science + Law (pre-law track). Schools like MIT, Princeton, and Georgetown are building dedicated programs around exactly this intersection. As AI gets deployed in healthcare, criminal justice, hiring, and finance, the need for specialists who can evaluate risks and build responsible frameworks is growing quickly.

13. Human-Centered UX/UI Design: Great design is deeply human. Understanding context, empathy, accessibility, and the way real people behave in digital spaces is something AI tools can assist with but cannot replace. UX/UI roles sit at the intersection of psychology, technology, and aesthetics — a combination that keeps them durable.

14. Technical Product Management: The rising value of technical product managers spans every domain — biotech, fintech, defense tech, climate tech, healthcare. Students who are technically literate but not hardcore coders, and who combine that with strong communication and strategic thinking, have a clear path into one of the most consistently high-demand roles in the modern economy. This is a field where a CS minor paired with a business or policy major can be more powerful than a CS degree alone.

15. Software & Cloud Architecture (Senior Track): The demand for senior software talent hasn’t declined; it’s increased. Engineers who can design complex, large-scale systems and infrastructure are more valuable than ever. The path here is longer than it used to be, but students who pursue CS with depth, specialize early, and build strong project portfolios can still reach this tier. The key word is differentiation: standing out requires more than a diploma.

The Unexpected Winners: Non-STEM Fields Rising in the AI Era

Here’s something that surprises many families: some of the most durable and newly advantaged career paths in an AI-driven economy aren’t in STEM at all. AI is actually increasing the value of certain non-technical disciplines — particularly those built on human judgment, relationships, creativity, and deep domain expertise that machines cannot replicate.

The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report makes this point clearly: AI literacy is growing faster than AI engineering skills across most industries, meaning that domain experts who understand how to work with AI are becoming more valuable in every field, not just tech.

1. Law — Especially Tech, IP, and AI Law: AI is creating an explosion of legal complexity around intellectual property, data privacy, liability, contracts, and regulation. Law schools are scrambling to build AI law curricula, and attorneys with fluency in both legal and technical domains are among the most sought-after professionals in the country. Pre-law students who study computer science, data science, or public policy alongside their humanities coursework will have an extraordinary advantage.

2. Healthcare & Medicine: Physician unemployment is essentially zero, and AI is making doctors more effective rather than replacing them. What’s changing is the nature of the work — physicians who understand how to interpret AI-assisted diagnostics, manage AI-driven treatment recommendations, and apply clinical judgment to machine-generated outputs will lead the field. Medicine remains one of the highest-earning, most recession-proof career paths available. Students aiming for medicine who also develop technical fluency will have a distinct advantage in research, hospital leadership, and health tech.

3. Psychology & Mental Health: There is a nationwide mental health crisis, a severe shortage of licensed therapists and counselors, and a growing consensus that human connection in mental healthcare is irreplaceable. AI tools are beginning to assist with intake, progress tracking, and psychoeducation — but the therapeutic relationship itself is deeply resistant to automation. Demand for clinical psychologists, licensed counselors, and social workers is projected to grow significantly over the next decade, with low unemployment and strong job security.

4. Education & Instructional Design: AI is transforming how learning happens, which creates enormous demand for people who understand both pedagogy and technology. Curriculum developers, instructional designers, learning experience designers, and education technologists who can shape how AI gets used in classrooms and corporate training environments are in a field that is growing, not shrinking. This is one of the most underrated career paths for students with both analytical and humanistic strengths.

5. Journalism & Communication (with Data Literacy): Counterintuitive but real: AI is simultaneously disrupting and elevating quality journalism. As AI-generated content floods the internet, the value of original reporting, investigative depth, human storytelling, and source relationships has actually increased. Journalists and communicators who combine traditional skills with data analysis, visualization, and AI tools are in a category of their own. Programs at Northwestern’s Medill School and Columbia Journalism School are producing graduates who command this intersection extremely well.

6. Business, Finance & Entrepreneurship: Finance and business are being transformed by AI — but the highest-value work in these fields has always been judgment, relationships, and strategy, none of which AI replicates well. Investment management, venture capital, corporate strategy, and entrepreneurship all remain human-centered at their core. What’s changing is that quantitative fluency is becoming a baseline expectation even in traditionally qualitative business roles — making the combination of business acumen and data literacy extremely powerful. Students pursuing business at schools like Wharton, Stern, Tepper, and Kelley who layer in AI tool fluency will be well ahead of their peers.

7. Philosophy, Ethics & the Humanities (as a Strategic Pairing): Perhaps the most counterintuitive entry on this list — but backed by real market evidence. The skills AI struggles most to replicate are precisely those developed by a rigorous humanities education: critical thinking, ethical reasoning, synthesis of ambiguous information, and the ability to communicate ideas persuasively. Philosophy majors are increasingly recruited by AI companies, policy organizations, and law schools. Mark Cuban has argued publicly that the students who will thrive in an AI economy are creative, analytical thinkers — including philosophy and liberal arts graduates. The key is pairing a humanities major with a technical minor or certificate in data science, CS, or policy. That combination is genuinely differentiated in ways a pure CS degree no longer is.

8. Architecture & Sustainable Design: AI is changing how buildings are designed, but it is not replacing the judgment, creativity, client relationships, and site-specific problem-solving that define great architecture. Meanwhile, the intersection of climate change and the built environment is creating entirely new specializations in sustainable design, net-zero construction, and urban resilience planning. Architecture programs with strong technology integration are producing graduates who are creatively and technically equipped for this moment in a way few other fields can match.

The Biggest Idea: Domain Expertise + AI Literacy Beats AI Engineering Alone for Most Students

The most important framing shift for families is this: for the majority of students, the goal is not to build AI — it’s to become the kind of professional who wields AI with deep expertise in their domain: A doctor who understands how to interpret AI diagnostics. A lawyer who can evaluate AI-generated contract language. A journalist who uses AI to analyze datasets. A psychologist who can distinguish between what AI-assisted tools can and cannot tell us about a patient. A business strategist who uses AI to model market scenarios and then makes the human calls about which path to take.

These are not niche roles — they are the mainstream of the professional economy in 2026 and beyond. The students who will thrive are not necessarily the ones who code the best. They are the ones who develop genuine expertise in a field, stay curious about technology, and build the adaptability to keep learning as the tools keep changing.

The Strategic Play for High Schoolers Today

Pursue depth over breadth. The market no longer rewards generalists. Students should identify a specialization early and build toward it intentionally — through coursework, extracurriculars, competitions, and summer programs.

Layer AI literacy onto any major. Whether a student is headed toward medicine, law, engineering, or the arts, understanding how AI tools work and how to use them meaningfully in their field is fast becoming a baseline professional expectation.

Consider the graduate school reality. In many high-value fields, a master’s degree or professional degree is increasingly the baseline. Families should plan for this possibility — both financially and in terms of college selection (schools with strong graduate programs and research opportunities matter more than they used to).

Build a portfolio, not just a transcript. In 2026, demonstrated work is increasingly more powerful than credentials alone. Projects, internships, research positions, and competition results signal capability in ways that grades no longer can on their own.

Start building your summer research and program record early. Selective summer programs at universities like Stanford, Brown, UChicago, Wharton, and Carnegie Mellon have become increasingly important signals of intellectual initiative and readiness — for both STEM and non-STEM applicants. Getting into the right programs takes the same strategic preparation as college applications themselves.

What This Looks Like in Practice: Blue Stars’ 2026 Results

This isn’t just theory. This June marks Blue Stars’ 16th year helping students navigate exactly these decisions — and this year’s results reflect the kind of strategic, differentiated planning the current landscape demands.

intro: What the CS Job Crisis Means for Your Child's Future Not long ago, a CS degree from Stanford was about as close to a guaranteed outcome as higher education offered. Tech companies recruited aggressively on campus. Signing bonuses were generous. Entry-level offers from Google, Meta, and Apple came easily. That era appears to be over, at least for now. The CS job crisis and the rapid evolution of future STEM careers are forcing families to rethink how students prepare for the modern economy. Stanford associate professor Jan Liphardt recently told the Los Angeles Times that graduates "are struggling to find entry-level jobs" at major tech companies. He considers it "a dramatic reversal from three years ago, when all of my undergraduate mentees found great jobs at the companies around us." The data backs him up. Employment among software developers aged 22–25 has fallen roughly 20% from its late-2022 peak, according to a Stanford Digital Economy Lab analysis of ADP payroll data. A Stanford study also found that entry-level hiring for AI-exposed jobs — roles for which AI can perform or assist with a significant share of the tasks involved, making human hires easier to reduce — declined 13% relative to less-exposed roles. Unemployment for CS graduates has climbed to around 6%, a level that would have seemed unthinkable just a few years ago. The shake-up isn't limited to Stanford. Students at UC Berkeley, USC, and schools across California are feeling it too, and the picture is even starker for graduates of less elite programs. What's Driving the CS Job Crisis? The easy narrative is: AI is taking CS jobs. The truth is more nuanced — and in some ways more important for families planning a college strategy. AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot have genuinely changed how software gets built. Managers who once staffed projects with ten junior developers can now achieve comparable output with two senior engineers and an AI assistant. That structural shift has hit entry-level roles hardest, because junior coders were traditionally doing exactly the kind of routine, repetitive programming that AI handles well. But there's also a macro-economic component. During the post-2020 zero-interest-rate period, tech companies went on massive hiring binges. Meta, for example, grew from roughly 45,000 to over 86,000 employees in three years. When the Fed raised rates aggressively starting in 2022, those same companies overcorrected, laying off tens of thousands and raising the bar for every new hire. New graduates entering that tightened market found themselves competing against experienced engineers who'd been let go. The result: a bifurcated job market where a small slice of graduates — those with deep AI skills, thick project portfolios, and real-world research experience — are landing good jobs, while everyone else is scrambling. Many Stanford students are now opting for a fifth-year master's program just to delay their job search and add credentials. As one graduate put it, "Half of my friends are still on campus doing their fifth-year master's." What This Means for High School College Planning For families, the real takeaway is this: general software programming is a surprisingly small corner of STEM, and it happens to be the corner AI is disrupting most. The rest of STEM tells a very different story. Fields like biomedical engineering, data science, robotics, and cybersecurity are projected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics to grow nearly three times faster than non-STEM roles through 2034. The question isn't whether to pursue STEM. It's which STEM path, and how to pursue it strategically. Here's what the data and current market conditions suggest are the strongest options for today's high schoolers. AI-Resilient STEM and Tech Paths Worth Pursuing 1. AI/ML Engineering & Research: The demand for people who can build and advance AI systems, not just use them, remains extremely strong. AI professionals earn between $96,000 and $200,000 per year, and some analysts project job growth of 26% over the coming decade. This is the field that's reshaping every other field. Students who want to go deep into CS should specialize here rather than pursuing general software engineering. 2. Cybersecurity: As AI-powered threats grow more sophisticated, so does the need for defenders. Cybersecurity is a national security priority, and the U.S. faces a significant shortage of skilled professionals in this area. Roles span risk assessment, security architecture, threat intelligence, and policy — giving students with varying strengths a range of entry points. The field is highly resistant to automation precisely because it requires adversarial, creative thinking that AI tools struggle to replicate. 3. Data Science & Business Intelligence: Data scientists and analysts sit at the intersection of technical skill and human judgment. AI can generate insights; humans still have to interpret them, communicate them to stakeholders, and make consequential decisions based on them. The market research and analytics field is projected to grow 34% over the next decade, with top earners exceeding $194,000 annually. 4. Robotics & Embedded Systems Engineering: Robotics is one of the most AI-resistant corners of the tech world, precisely because it requires making AI work in messy, unpredictable physical environments. The field is growing 9–13% annually. Top programs are at Carnegie Mellon, MIT, Georgia Tech, and Michigan. Students who like the intersection of hardware and software, building things that interact with the real world, are well suited here. 5. Electrical & Computer Engineering (with AI Specialization): Traditional electrical engineering such as power systems, control systems, semiconductor design remains deeply valuable and relatively insulated from the current AI disruption. Pairing an ECE foundation with machine learning coursework positions students for roles in chip design, autonomous systems, and industrial automation that are difficult to automate away. 6. Biomedical Engineering & Health Tech: The combination of an aging population, a growing healthcare system, and the rapid deployment of AI in medicine creates enormous demand for engineers who understand both biology and technology. Nursing holds the lowest unemployment rate of any degree at 2.1%, and biomedical fields adjacent to healthcare show similarly strong job security. 7. Bioinformatics & Computational Biology: One of the fastest-growing and most underappreciated intersections in all of STEM. Bioinformatics combines biology, statistics, and programming to analyze genomic data, model disease, and accelerate drug discovery — and it is specifically highlighted in the Stanford 2026 AI Index as a resilient growth area. Students with interests in both life sciences and data are unusually well positioned here. This is one of the few fields where being a skilled programmer and a skilled biologist is genuinely additive rather than redundant. 8. Quantum Computing: Still early-stage, but attracting enormous investment from Google, IBM, Microsoft, and the federal government. The talent pipeline is almost empty at the entry level, meaning students who build quantum literacy now will face far less competition than in any other emerging field. Students pursuing physics or applied math who develop quantum literacy will be poised for roles that will be in extremely high demand within the decade. 9. Nuclear Engineering: A field experiencing a genuine renaissance. With major tech companies like Google and Microsoft signing contracts for nuclear energy to power their data centers, and the federal government investing heavily in next-generation reactor design, nuclear engineers are in high demand for the first time in a generation. It's one of the most durable and physically irreplaceable engineering disciplines. 10. Environmental & Civil Engineering: Infrastructure is having a moment. Federal investment in roads, bridges, power grids, and water systems is driving sustained demand for civil engineers (projected 7–8% growth), who work on projects that are inherently local, physical, and resistant to remote or AI-driven displacement. Environmental engineering adds the additional tailwind of clean energy transition and climate adaptation work. 11. Supply Chain & Operations Engineering (Industrial Engineering): Underappreciated and highly employable. Industrial and systems engineers who specialize in supply chain optimization and operations are in strong demand at companies like Amazon, Apple, and major manufacturers, with work that is AI-augmented rather than AI-displaced. These roles require the kind of systems thinking and process judgment that AI tools currently support but cannot replace. 12. AI Ethics, Governance & Policy: Best pursued as a combined or double major rather than a standalone — think CS + Philosophy, Data Science + Public Policy, or Computer Science + Law (pre-law track). Schools like MIT, Princeton, and Georgetown are building dedicated programs around exactly this intersection. As AI gets deployed in healthcare, criminal justice, hiring, and finance, the need for specialists who can evaluate risks and build responsible frameworks is growing quickly. 13. Human-Centered UX/UI Design: Great design is deeply human. Understanding context, empathy, accessibility, and the way real people behave in digital spaces is something AI tools can assist with but cannot replace. UX/UI roles sit at the intersection of psychology, technology, and aesthetics — a combination that keeps them durable. 14. Technical Product Management: The rising value of technical product managers spans every domain — biotech, fintech, defense tech, climate tech, healthcare. Students who are technically literate but not hardcore coders, and who combine that with strong communication and strategic thinking, have a clear path into one of the most consistently high-demand roles in the modern economy. This is a field where a CS minor paired with a business or policy major can be more powerful than a CS degree alone. 15. Software & Cloud Architecture (Senior Track): The demand for senior software talent hasn't declined; it's increased. Engineers who can design complex, large-scale systems and infrastructure are more valuable than ever. The path here is longer than it used to be, but students who pursue CS with depth, specialize early, and build strong project portfolios can still reach this tier. The key word is differentiation: standing out requires more than a diploma. The Unexpected Winners: Non-STEM Fields Rising in the AI Era Here's something that surprises many families: some of the most durable and newly advantaged career paths in an AI-driven economy aren't in STEM at all. AI is actually increasing the value of certain non-technical disciplines — particularly those built on human judgment, relationships, creativity, and deep domain expertise that machines cannot replicate. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report makes this point clearly: AI literacy is growing faster than AI engineering skills across most industries, meaning that domain experts who understand how to work with AI are becoming more valuable in every field, not just tech. 1. Law — Especially Tech, IP, and AI Law: AI is creating an explosion of legal complexity around intellectual property, data privacy, liability, contracts, and regulation. Law schools are scrambling to build AI law curricula, and attorneys with fluency in both legal and technical domains are among the most sought-after professionals in the country. Pre-law students who study computer science, data science, or public policy alongside their humanities coursework will have an extraordinary advantage. 2. Healthcare & Medicine: Physician unemployment is essentially zero, and AI is making doctors more effective rather than replacing them. What's changing is the nature of the work — physicians who understand how to interpret AI-assisted diagnostics, manage AI-driven treatment recommendations, and apply clinical judgment to machine-generated outputs will lead the field. Medicine remains one of the highest-earning, most recession-proof career paths available. Students aiming for medicine who also develop technical fluency will have a distinct advantage in research, hospital leadership, and health tech. 3. Psychology & Mental Health: There is a nationwide mental health crisis, a severe shortage of licensed therapists and counselors, and a growing consensus that human connection in mental healthcare is irreplaceable. AI tools are beginning to assist with intake, progress tracking, and psychoeducation — but the therapeutic relationship itself is deeply resistant to automation. Demand for clinical psychologists, licensed counselors, and social workers is projected to grow significantly over the next decade, with low unemployment and strong job security. 4. Education & Instructional Design: AI is transforming how learning happens, which creates enormous demand for people who understand both pedagogy and technology. Curriculum developers, instructional designers, learning experience designers, and education technologists who can shape how AI gets used in classrooms and corporate training environments are in a field that is growing, not shrinking. This is one of the most underrated career paths for students with both analytical and humanistic strengths. 5. Journalism & Communication (with Data Literacy): Counterintuitive but real: AI is simultaneously disrupting and elevating quality journalism. As AI-generated content floods the internet, the value of original reporting, investigative depth, human storytelling, and source relationships has actually increased. Journalists and communicators who combine traditional skills with data analysis, visualization, and AI tools are in a category of their own. Programs at Northwestern's Medill School and Columbia Journalism School are producing graduates who command this intersection extremely well. 6. Business, Finance & Entrepreneurship: Finance and business are being transformed by AI — but the highest-value work in these fields has always been judgment, relationships, and strategy, none of which AI replicates well. Investment management, venture capital, corporate strategy, and entrepreneurship all remain human-centered at their core. What's changing is that quantitative fluency is becoming a baseline expectation even in traditionally qualitative business roles — making the combination of business acumen and data literacy extremely powerful. Students pursuing business at schools like Wharton, Stern, Tepper, and Kelley who layer in AI tool fluency will be well ahead of their peers. 7. Philosophy, Ethics & the Humanities (as a Strategic Pairing): Perhaps the most counterintuitive entry on this list — but backed by real market evidence. The skills AI struggles most to replicate are precisely those developed by a rigorous humanities education: critical thinking, ethical reasoning, synthesis of ambiguous information, and the ability to communicate ideas persuasively. Philosophy majors are increasingly recruited by AI companies, policy organizations, and law schools. Mark Cuban has argued publicly that the students who will thrive in an AI economy are creative, analytical thinkers — including philosophy and liberal arts graduates. The key is pairing a humanities major with a technical minor or certificate in data science, CS, or policy. That combination is genuinely differentiated in ways a pure CS degree no longer is. 8. Architecture & Sustainable Design: AI is changing how buildings are designed, but it is not replacing the judgment, creativity, client relationships, and site-specific problem-solving that define great architecture. Meanwhile, the intersection of climate change and the built environment is creating entirely new specializations in sustainable design, net-zero construction, and urban resilience planning. Architecture programs with strong technology integration are producing graduates who are creatively and technically equipped for this moment in a way few other fields can match. The Biggest Idea: Domain Expertise + AI Literacy Beats AI Engineering Alone for Most Students The most important framing shift for families is this: for the majority of students, the goal is not to build AI — it's to become the kind of professional who wields AI with deep expertise in their domain: A doctor who understands how to interpret AI diagnostics. A lawyer who can evaluate AI-generated contract language. A journalist who uses AI to analyze datasets. A psychologist who can distinguish between what AI-assisted tools can and cannot tell us about a patient. A business strategist who uses AI to model market scenarios and then makes the human calls about which path to take. These are not niche roles — they are the mainstream of the professional economy in 2026 and beyond. The students who will thrive are not necessarily the ones who code the best. They are the ones who develop genuine expertise in a field, stay curious about technology, and build the adaptability to keep learning as the tools keep changing. The Strategic Play for High Schoolers Today Pursue depth over breadth. The market no longer rewards generalists. Students should identify a specialization early and build toward it intentionally — through coursework, extracurriculars, competitions, and summer programs. Layer AI literacy onto any major. Whether a student is headed toward medicine, law, engineering, or the arts, understanding how AI tools work and how to use them meaningfully in their field is fast becoming a baseline professional expectation. Consider the graduate school reality. In many high-value fields, a master's degree or professional degree is increasingly the baseline. Families should plan for this possibility — both financially and in terms of college selection (schools with strong graduate programs and research opportunities matter more than they used to). Build a portfolio, not just a transcript. In 2026, demonstrated work is increasingly more powerful than credentials alone. Projects, internships, research positions, and competition results signal capability in ways that grades no longer can on their own. Start building your summer research and program record early. Selective summer programs at universities like Stanford, Brown, UChicago, Wharton, and Carnegie Mellon have become increasingly important signals of intellectual initiative and readiness — for both STEM and non-STEM applicants. title: The Harvard-Educated Counselor Who Keeps Getting Students Into Harvard and Stanford
excerpt: Helen Ingerson doesn't just know what it takes to get into Harvard — she's lived it. A Harvard graduate herself and a cornerstone of the Blue Stars team for over a decade, Helen has built a…

author.name: Helen Ingerson
author.bio: Helen Ingerson is a Harvard University graduate and master college consultant who has guided Blue Stars students to Harvard, Stanford, and premier institutions.

contentHtml:
Helen Ingerson doesn’t just know what it takes to get into Harvard — she’s lived it. A Harvard graduate herself and a cornerstone of the Blue Stars team for over a decade, Helen has built a remarkable track record: year after year, her students earn admission to the most selective universities in the world, including Harvard and Stanford. Dr. M sat down with Helen to find out what she sees, how she works, and what it really takes.

Helen Ingerson, Harvard Graduate & Senior Admissions Counselor at Blue Stars

DrM: You graduated from Harvard. How does that experience shape the way you counsel students today?

Helen: It helps me know how to counsel students who would – and wouldn’t – perhaps find Harvard to be a “fit” for them. Like many large universities, Harvard offers a stunning array of academic resources and opportunities. But that can also mean it’s an overwhelming environment for students who are not “self-starters,” know what interests them, and/or have the confidence to go out and find the resources that will help them address and pursue their passions.

The Harvard admissions process also typically selects for students with multiple leadership roles that show deep commitment to a few activities in depth, rewarding students who are fairly extroverted, so that once they arrive on campus, they have the confidence to network, find, and create their own opportunities because at a large university, no one is holding a student’s hand to help them figure out what they want to do. People will certainly respond if you tell them what you need or want, but they’re not “scouting” for students interested in fellowships or opportunities the way they might be at a smaller school. So I can advise students whose personalities do, and don’t, match these attributes, and help them understand what to “build into” their high school years if Harvard is one of the schools they’re aiming for.

DrM: When you first meet a student, what are you trying to understand about them?

Helen: What their core interests and capabilities are – that is, what they are truly interested in, as opposed to what they think or have been told they should want to do. This is because I’m always thinking down the road on their behalf – to the fall of their senior year when they have to present a coherent story to an admissions officer in their college applications and essays. That can seem a long way away for a 9th grader, but it’s always in the back of my mind: what do they need to be doing now? What next?

This way, they can build their story a step at a time. Often, that requires gaining the concrete skills that will enable them to pursue the next step at a more advanced level: learning wet lab skills this year so that the next year they can offer those skills to a university professor to help with their research. Or programming skills, so that they can delve into a complex AI-based robotics project.

I always have the “road map” in my mind for them on their behalf, helping them build their application profile. The more I know about what truly interests them, the more I can help them create a profile based on these because they’ll have a higher level of commitment and interest if they’re pursuing and engaging in activities that really matter to them. And this means they’ll be able to demonstrate true commitment to those interests in their applications, putting in the time and effort to those activities that admissions officers expect to see, and probably reaching the higher levels of responsibility (officer positions, recognition) in those activities that can also be rewarded in the admissions process.

DrM: How do you help a student uncover what makes them genuinely compelling — not just on paper, but as a person?

Helen: We have extensive conversations about their classes and activities so that I can ask guiding questions about what really interests them about their activities. If a student likes to coach swimming, for example, what is it ABOUT that they truly enjoy – is it the biomechanics they observe? Uncovering and unlocking how to motivate a younger child? If it’s the first, they may be interested in the biomedical field. As I find activities and summer programs and community service/volunteering opportunities that enable them to pursue those interests, I can find out more and more about what they really want to do through their reactions to what I find in preparatory meetings. We may focus on research into orthopedics or volunteering to help children with physical challenges if they are fascinated by watching and studying the biomechanics of swimming. If what they like about coaching swimming is motivating children to learn, that may lead to our focusing on developmental or educational psychology.

If a student pursues an activity because they think they “should” but don’t really enjoy it, that typically becomes pretty obvious fairly quickly – they don’t offer a lot of information about what they’re doing and don’t devote much time to it. But when they get excited about a school project or something they’re doing, I pick up on that on their behalf and we run with it. The method is to dig into specificities with each student to tailor their multi-year journey in a way that is most fitting and fulfilling to them.

DrM: How do you handle a student who’s talented but doesn’t yet believe in themselves?

Helen: I always try to break large projects or decisions into smaller steps, having students accomplish the preliminary, beginning phases successfully so that they can then tackle something more complex that may take more initiative, confidence, or creativity down the line.

As an example, one student wanted to develop a nonprofit to combat scientific misinformation. She started by thinking through whether she would do this through a club or website, with whom and with how many peers. Did she even know responsible peers who would be a help to her in building an initiative like this, or would she have to find them? What would the sections of a website be, and what would attract users? Then she reached out to others who might be interested, and designed the website. Next, during a summer program she got students from across the country involved, and even contacted college professors in the field to contribute to their efforts.

So by the time she applied to Stanford, she had established a national organization with chapters across multiple states. She was accepted to Stanford REA.

It is also important to offer students different options for demonstrating their interests in a way that is comfortable for them. If a student plays piano, they could teach younger, under-resourced students. But if they don’t enjoy teaching, they could instead hold concerts to help raise funds for organizations, causes, and issues they believe in or play for senior homes. If they’re not wild about performing in public, maybe they’re interested in composing their own music and/or working with a mentor to develop a portfolio of compositions.

So it’s important to adapt and change direction to match the student’s capabilities with their personality and resources – including whether they know peers to work with to start or grow some kind of original initiative, or whether they need or want to do something on their own. For example, one student developed a bilingual book club and then summer program for students at a local public library, and another developed an original curriculum to teach essay/critical reading and thinking classes for students whose parents couldn’t afford extracurricular classes. Neither worked with other students on these projects, but both were accepted to schools they were excited about attending.

DrM: What’s the most common thing you find yourself fixing or redirecting in a student’s application?

Helen: Students often answer essay questions without understanding that every essay is a chance to convince a college to accept them. This often involves a delicate balance of personal revelation vs. explaining and including personal achievements in a kind of writing students are not familiar with. Sometimes, if a college asks about a challenge a student has overcome, a teen writer is very open and honest about some very personal issue they’ve had – when the college really wants to know what they did to solve that issue, not all the very emotional detail teens will often include about how unpleasant or difficult the experience was for them.

On the other hand, students (and parents…) can sometimes see essays as functionally the same as a resume: a place to recite every achievement the student has under their belt. That’s not really going to make an appealing essay, and it can often come through to an admissions officer as “braggy.”

I sometimes tell students to think of essays as if they are a lawyer standing in front of a jury making an admissions case for themselves. They need to think about how what they write makes them sound authentically interested in studying something, what it is they eventually want to do with that knowledge, how the resources at that school will contribute to their achieving their goals, and also demonstrate their own personality and why things they’ve done matter to them.

But it’s also important for students to write about not just what they will get OUT of a school, but what they will contribute TO it – something students often don’t think much about. So in general, college essays may be the first time students truly have to think not only about expressing themselves, but the audience they are writing for, and how that audience will interpret and react to what they’ve written.

DrM: What do most families misunderstand about what Harvard and Stanford are actually looking for?

Helen: Families often think that college admissions is a “numbers game” and that they remain solely focused on top scores and grades. All things being equal, of course these things help, and give these schools fewer reasons to “screen a student out” of admissions consideration.

So I like to show students and families admissions scatterplots revealing GPA graphed against standardized test scores, which illustrate that yes, students with high GPAs and scores do gain admission. But there are also always some students in the bottom lefthand corner with low grades and scores who were also admitted, and students in the upper righthand corner with high scores and grades who were not. After all, the bottom 25th percentile SAT or ACT score of the class for any school means that a full one-quarter of that school’s entering class was selected from among a pool of applicants with those 25th percentile scores – or below those scores. OR BELOW.

Most colleges “assemble an orchestra” of students, each of whom has their own interests, and admissions can often reflect what each school is looking for that specific year. One year, they may have many more Neuroscience applicants so that year admissions might be more difficult if a student indicates an interest in that major. They might also have very few applicants who want to major in History, so may accept more students who indicate that interest that year.

So rather than trying to “guess” what a school may look for, it’s important to remember that students who have meaningful commitments and interests and have pursued these are always valued by admissions officers, who will assume that anything a student has spent time on in high school is important to them: the more time students spend on an activity or pursuing an area of academic interest, the more an admissions officer will understand that as a priority for that student.

When it comes to Stanford and Harvard, there really aren’t “external” quantifiable, specific lists of achievements or activities, but there are characteristics and attributes rewarded by admissions committees. The more time a student has spent, the “higher level” of participation these schools assume they will achieve: officer/leadership positions, initiating projects, achievements/competitions at a national or international level in the activities and fields that interest them. So no, neither school is “looking for” something as specific as participation in Debate; or whether a student plays an instrument AND a sport AND volunteered for X number of hours; or whether they took a specific number of AP courses.

DrM: The students who get the best results — what do they have in common?

Helen: They have a combination of breadth and depth.

Depth in terms of about three major “themes” in what they’ve pursued in high school: an academic interest they have pursued; one, two, or three extracurricular activities where they have achieved officer positions or launched initiatives that demonstrate their commitment to an issue, problem or cause the student cares about and spent time on, which demonstrates commitment; and some kind of committed community service that says they care about more than “just being good at things” or their own personal achievement.

The breadth comes from a sprinkling of other interests – sports, music, clubs they’ve participated in but don’t run or haven’t founded – but which show that these students are multi-dimensional and interested in and curious about perspectives outside of their main interests. And an academic track record that says they know how to work hard, like to challenge themselves, and perform at a high level.

DrM: What would you tell a family starting in 9th grade about how to make the most of the years ahead?

Helen: To work toward building an admissions profile one step at a time – start to work toward defining your student’s academic interests because colleges look for students who have demonstrated their interests in the majors they indicate on their applications. Encourage your student to take classes, pursue projects, and/or participate in programs that interest them.

But don’t be afraid to change course if the student changes their mind. I’ve worked with two students who both thought they were interested in astronomy and/or astrobiology in 9th grade. Each took a summer course about these fields, but neither ended up wanting to study anything in that field: one ended up interested in developmental psychology, and the other, business.

Have your student also start to explore volunteering they can do at their age and that interests them – not just to “check the box” of how many hours of community service they have done (the number of hours doesn’t really tell a college anything about an applicant other than the fact that they can count) but because what colleges really look at is what a student’s volunteering says about what the applicant cares about. If a student volunteers doing something that interests them, they’re much more likely to “stick with it” and then achieve more, either through taking on more responsibility within an organization or launching their own initiative in that area.

The key to successful top college admissions isn’t about following a formula – “Everyone at my high school who was admitted to Harvard was on the Debate Team,” or “All of my friends’ children admitted to Stanford played piano” – but building a cohesive collection of experiences a student has engaged in throughout high school that demonstrate what matters to the applicant.

The earlier a student starts on this journey, the more time they have to change course if that happens, and still develop a full, comprehensive and coherent story that tells a college that if something matters to them, they explore and pursue it.

intro: Helen Ingerson doesn't just know what it takes to get into Harvard — she's lived it. Dr. M sat down with Helen to find out what she sees, how she works, and what it really takes. Helen Ingerson, Harvard Graduate & Senior Admissions Counselor at Blue Stars DrM: You graduated from Harvard. How does that experience shape the way you counsel students today? Helen: It helps me know how to counsel students who would – and wouldn’t – perhaps find Harvard to be a “fit” for them. Like many large universities, Harvard offers a stunning array of academic resources and opportunities. But that can also mean it’s an overwhelming environment for students who are not “self-starters,” know what interests them, and/or have the confidence to go out and find the resources that will help them address and pursue their passions. The Harvard admissions process also typically selects for students with multiple leadership roles that show deep commitment to a few activities in depth, rewarding students who are fairly extroverted, so that once they arrive on campus, they have the confidence to network, find, and create their own opportunities because at a large university, no one is holding a student’s hand to help them figure out what they want to do. People will certainly respond if you tell them what you need or want, but they’re not “scouting” for students interested in fellowships or opportunities the way they might be at a smaller school. So I can advise students whose personalities do, and don’t, match these attributes, and help them understand what to “build into” their high school years if Harvard is one of the schools they’re aiming for. DrM: When you first meet a student, what are you trying to understand about them? Helen: What their core interests and capabilities are – that is, what they are truly interested in, as opposed to what they think or have been told they should want to do. This is because I’m always thinking down the road on their behalf – to the fall of their senior year when they have to present a coherent story to an admissions officer in their college applications and essays. That can seem a long way away for a 9th grader, but it’s always in the back of my mind: what do they need to be doing now? What next? This way, they can build their story a step at a time. Often, that requires gaining the concrete skills that will enable them to pursue the next step at a more advanced level: learning wet lab skills this year so that the next year they can offer those skills to a university professor to help with their research. Or programming skills, so that they can delve into a complex AI-based robotics project. I always have the “road map” in my mind for them on their behalf, helping them build their application profile. The more I know about what truly interests them, the more I can help them create a profile based on these because they’ll have a higher level of commitment and interest if they’re pursuing and engaging in activities that really matter to them. And this means they’ll be able to demonstrate true commitment to those interests in their applications, putting in the time and effort to those activities that admissions officers expect to see, and probably reaching the higher levels of responsibility (officer positions, recognition) in those activities that can also be rewarded in the admissions process. DrM: How do you help a student uncover what makes them genuinely compelling — not just on paper, but as a person? Helen: We have extensive conversations about their classes and activities so that I can ask guiding questions about what really interests them about their activities. If a student likes to coach swimming, for example, what is it ABOUT that they truly enjoy – is it the biomechanics they observe? Uncovering and unlocking how to motivate a younger child? If it’s the first, they may be interested in the biomedical field. As I find activities and summer programs and community service/volunteering opportunities that enable them to pursue those interests, I can find out more and more about what they really want to do through their reactions to what I find in preparatory meetings. We may focus on research into orthopedics or volunteering to help children with physical challenges if they are fascinated by watching and studying the biomechanics of swimming. If what they like about coaching swimming is motivating children to learn, that may lead to our focusing on developmental or educational psychology. If a student pursues an activity because they think they “should” but don’t really enjoy it, that typically becomes pretty obvious fairly quickly – they don’t offer a lot of information about what they’re doing and don’t devote much time to it. But when they get excited about a school project or something they’re doing, I pick up on that on their behalf and we run with it. The method is to dig into specificities with each student to tailor their multi-year journey in a way that is most fitting and fulfilling to them. DrM: How do you handle a student who’s talented but doesn’t yet believe in themselves? Helen: I always try to break large projects or decisions into smaller steps, having students accomplish the preliminary, beginning phases successfully so that they can then tackle something more complex that may take more initiative, confidence, or creativity down the line. As an example, one student wanted to develop a nonprofit to combat scientific misinformation. She started by thinking through whether she would do this through a club or website, with whom and with how many peers. Did she even know responsible peers who would be a help to her in building an initiative like this, or would she have to find them? What would the sections of a website be, and what would attract users? Then she reached out to others who might be interested, and designed the website. Next, during a summer program she got students from across the country involved, and even contacted college professors in the field to contribute to their efforts. So by the time she applied to Stanford, she had established a national organization with chapters across multiple states. She was accepted to Stanford REA. It is also important to offer students different options for demonstrating their interests in a way that is comfortable for them. But if they don’t enjoy teaching, they could instead hold concerts to help raise funds for organizations, causes, and issues they believe in or play for senior homes. So it’s important to adapt and change direction to match the student’s capabilities with their personality and resources – including whether they know peers to work with to start or grow some kind of original initiative, or whether they need or want to do something on their own. Helen: Students often answer essay questions without understanding that every essay is a chance to convince a college to accept them. This often involves a delicate balance of personal revelation vs. explaining and including personal achievements in a kind of writing students are not familiar with. Sometimes, if a college asks about a challenge a student has overcome, a teen writer is very open and honest about some very personal issue they’ve had – when the college really wants to know what they did to solve that issue, not all the very emotional detail teens will often include about how unpleasant or difficult the experience was for them. On the other hand, students (and parents…) can sometimes see essays as functionally the same as a resume: a place to recite every achievement the student has under their belt. That’s not really going to make an appealing essay, and it can often come through to an admissions officer as “braggy.” I sometimes tell students to think of essays as if they are a lawyer standing in front of a jury making an admissions case for themselves. But it’s also important for students to write about not just what they will get OUT of a school, but what they will contribute TO it – something students often don’t think much about. Helen: Families often think that college admissions is a “numbers game” and that they remain solely focused on top scores and grades. All things being equal, of course these things help, and give these schools fewer reasons to “screen a student out” of admissions consideration. But there are also always some students in the bottom lefthand corner with low grades and scores who were also admitted, and students in the upper righthand corner with high scores and grades who were not. After all, the bottom 25th percentile SAT or ACT score of the class for any school means that a full one-quarter of that school’s entering class was selected from among a pool of applicants with those 25th percentile scores – or below those scores. OR BELOW. Most colleges “assemble an orchestra” of students, each of whom has their own interests, and admissions can often reflect what each school is looking for that specific year. title: Harvard, Stanford, CMU, NYU & More: Blue Stars 2026 Admissions Results

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
Strategic Planning. Bold Vision. Brilliant Outcomes | Blue Stars College Admissions Results 2026

Every year, we say it: the results speak for themselves. And every year, our students prove it again.

The Class of 2026 delivered some of the most impressive admissions outcomes in Blue Stars history. Harvard. Stanford. Northwestern. Georgetown. Cornell ED. CMU’s School of Computer Science ED. NYU Stern ED. WashU ED. Plus elite liberal arts admits to Pomona, Williams, and Swarthmore, scholarships worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, and one of our strongest pre-college program hauls yet.

These aren’t lottery wins. They’re the result of years of intentional strategy, authentic storytelling, and the courage to aim high.

Why Early Decision (ED) Matters

ED isn’t right for every student — but when it is, the results can be transformative. This year’s ED wins demonstrate exactly what happens when a student is clear on their first choice and has built a truly competitive application.

We’re thrilled to announce:

  • Cornell University (ED) – Engineering
  • CMU School of Computer Science (ED) — one of the most selective CS programs in the world
  • CMU Tepper School of Business (ED) — recruited for soccer
  • WashU (ED) — student’s first choice
  • NYU Stern School of Business (ED)

These students had clear goals, well-crafted applications, and started working with us early enough to position themselves strategically.

A Comprehensive Strategy Yields Powerful Results

Beyond ED, our students earned admission to an extraordinary range of top universities this cycle. Some standout offers include:

  • Harvard University
  • Stanford University
  • Northwestern University
  • Georgetown University
  • Pomona College, Williams College, Swarthmore College — three of the nation’s top liberal arts colleges
  • UC Berkeley — multiple admits, including the elite MET.ai Tech + Business Program
  • UCLA, UCSD, UCSB, UC Davis, UC Irvine, UC Santa Cruz — strong UC representation across the board
  • University of Michigan — multiple admits
  • University of Virginia, UIUC, University of Wisconsin – Madison
  • Harvey Mudd College, Emory University
  • UT Austin — including the prestigious Turing Scholars CS Honors Program
  • Purdue University — multiple admits
  • University of Washington, Georgia Tech, Case Western Reserve
  • Northeastern University — with merit scholarship ($5K/semester)
  • Indiana University — direct admit to the Kelley School of Business
  • University of Toronto, McGill University
  • Pratt Institute, OTIS College of Art and Design

From CS to business, public policy to biomedical engineering, the arts to neuroscience — our students matched with schools that align with their unique strengths and long-term aspirations.

Scholarship Highlights

Our students didn’t just get in — they earned exceptional financial recognition:

  • Santa Clara University — $130,000 over 4 years (50% off tuition) + Honors Program invitation
  • University of Minnesota Honors College — $20,000/year National Scholarship for 4 years
  • Northeastern University — $5,000/semester merit scholarship

Summer & Enrichment Programs: A Launchpad for Success

The admits above didn’t come out of nowhere. They were years in the making — and a big part of that story is the competitive summer and enrichment programs our students participated in. These experiences deepen intellectual curiosity, confirm academic direction, and give admissions readers compelling evidence of initiative and seriousness.

Here are just a few of this year’s highlights:

Research & STEM:

  • Stanford SASI (Anesthesia Summer Institute)
  • Stanford PIPS, Stanford SIMR
  • Stanford CNI-X Neuroscience Program
  • Stanford SHTEM
  • Berkeley Labs Internship
  • UCSB Summer Research Academies (SRA) — multiple admits
  • UCSB Research Mentorship Program (RMP)
  • COSMOS (UC System) — multiple admits
  • UCSC Science Internship Program (SIP)
  • UT Austin SEES
  • NASA Research Program
  • UCLA Game Lab
  • Roberts Cancer Fellowship
  • ASDRP Spring Research Program

Business, Humanities & Leadership:

  • Wharton Essentials of Entrepreneurship
  • Iacocca Global Entrepreneurship Intensive
  • Columbia Summer Immersion — Developmental Economics & Quantitative Public Policy
  • Columbia SHAPE Program
  • UChicago Summer Immersion — Quantitative Analysis of Public Policy
  • Summer@Brown
  • Brown Leadership Institute
  • Georgetown Marketing and Personal Branding Academy
  • Tufts Marketing Academy
  • UPenn ESAP & Experimental Physics Research Academy
  • Juilliard Summer — Composing (accepted!)

Pre-Professional:

  • University of the Pacific Summer Dental Program

Graduate School, Too

Blue Stars supports students at every stage. This cycle, we also helped a graduate school applicant earn admission to Alliant International University’s Counseling Program.

Start Early. Dream Big. Execute with Intention.

The takeaway from this banner year? Start early and stay intentional. The most successful students began their journey with Blue Stars as early as 8th or 9th grade, giving us time to shape a trajectory of growth, depth, and leadership — not just for college, but for life.

In today’s highly selective admissions environment, a last-minute scramble just won’t cut it. Building a strong narrative requires years of exploration, reflection, and action — and we’re here to guide every step.

To Our Students: Congratulations!

Every single one of you showed up, did the work, and had the courage to go after what you wanted. You’ve proven that strategy and soul go hand in hand — and we can’t wait to see what’s next for each of you.

Here’s to the Class of 2026 — and beyond.

Want your student to be part of next year’s success story?

Our 2026 results weren’t a coincidence — they were the result of early engagement, strategic planning, and a commitment to growth. If your family is ready to take the first step toward a personalized admissions strategy with proven results, now’s the time to begin.

Contact us today to start building your student’s path to college success.
