author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
As we approach our 16th anniversary at Blue Stars Admissions Consulting, we’re filled with gratitude for the many remarkable stories we’ve helped students shape over the years. Guiding teens in capturing their true selves in writing — while discovering their passions, quirks, and quiet strengths along the way — has been a true privilege. 

Our work with students all begins with an open-ended free-writing activity, during which we help students dig deep to uncover topics that not only highlight their talents but also build confidence and pride in who they are. Our favorite part, though, is bringing essays to life through careful and joyful editing, teaching students to embrace writing and revising as a process. When finished, Blue Stars students walk away not only with polished applications but a skill set that empowers them in college and beyond.

Here, we’re excited to share highlights of some of our most successful essays written by STEM students who gained admission to the top 20 universities, offering a glimpse into the unique journeys, beliefs, and insights that made each student unforgettable to admissions officers at these elite institutions.

Courage in Advocacy: Example Essays on Standing Up for Beliefs

These essays reveal the bravery it takes to challenge the status quo and stand up for what’s right. Top schools value students who demonstrate courage and resilience because they seek individuals who will positively impact their campus and the world beyond, showing integrity and commitment to advocate for change.

  • Taking a Stand for a Classmate: When Ethan learned that a group of classmates had elected a shy peer to be Homecoming Queen as a prank, he felt compelled to act. Instead of allowing her to face ridicule, Ethan volunteered to be her escort, fully aware that his decision might invite teasing or even backlash. Through spending time with his classmate, he discovered her to be a fascinating, talented person with unique strengths. This experience deepened his commitment to inclusivity and motivated him to promote a culture of respect and acceptance as a leader of his school’s literary magazine. Ethan’s essay stood out because of its powerful depiction of courage and integrity in the face of peer pressure. His story revealed a genuine sense of empathy and commitment to others, qualities highly valued by admissions officers.
  • Creating Safe Spaces in the Face of Opposition: Sophia’s presentation in favor of affirmative action in her American History class sparked intense pushback from classmates, many of whom held opposing views on the topic. Although criticism could have discouraged her, Sophia was motivated instead to act on her convictions. She founded an LGBTQ safe space club at her school to provide support for students who, like herself, had felt marginalized. This experience led her to the UPenn Social Justice Academy, where she learned new approaches to advocacy. Sophia’s dedication even caught the attention of a Yale admissions officer who praised her resilience and dedication to social justice. Her essay succeeded because it showed her as a change-maker unafraid of controversy, able to create meaningful impact through compassion, leadership, and a strong sense of purpose.

Exploring Identity: Essays on Cultural Heritage and Personal Transformation

These essays reflect the complex journeys students take as they explore their cultural heritage through self-discovery. Admissions officers appreciate students who bring unique perspectives and self-awareness to their applications, as they enrich the campus community and inspire deeper discussions on identity and diversity.

  • Reclaiming a Lost Heritage: Noah’s essay explored his journey to reconnect with his Japanese heritage, which had been partially lost in his family in America during WWII. Feeling caught between his Chinese and Japanese cultural backgrounds, Noah decided to study Japanese language and culture in a search for belonging and identity. His essay vividly described how his Japanese name, once a source of confusion, became a point of pride and personal history as he came to understand more about his roots. Noah’s essay was successful because it conveyed his self-awareness and his dedication to embracing his heritage, showing a student willing to reconcile complex aspects of identity. Admissions officers were drawn to Noah’s honesty and the depth of his journey toward self-acceptance.
  • Challenging Stereotypes of Asian Identity: When Hannah’s family faced unexpected challenges, including her parents’ divorce and financial difficulties, she began questioning the stereotypes she had previously accepted about her Asian heritage. Reflecting on her childhood, Hannah realized that she had subconsciously placed herself in a box defined by cultural expectations. Her essay traced her journey toward seeing herself as an individual first, someone shaped by a unique set of circumstances rather than by a single narrative. Her essay was compelling because it addressed a universal theme—questioning self-imposed labels—through a deeply personal lens, highlighting her growth in self-definition. Admissions officers admired her courage to confront ingrained beliefs and her determination to live authentically.

Literature as a Lens: Essays Inspired by Books and Authors

These essays reveal how literature can shape a student’s worldview and personal character. Top schools value students who draw insight from literature because it signals a capacity for critical thinking, empathy, and reflection—qualities essential for contributing meaningfully to a vibrant academic environment.

  • Finding Meaning in Classic Literature: Maya didn’t expect 19th-century literature to change her life, yet the works of Jane Austen and other classic authors resonated with her on a profound level. In her essay, she described how these novels taught her the value of precision, thoughtfulness, and depth, qualities she began to recognize in herself. Maya saw herself reflected in Austen’s characters, who balance personal integrity with social expectations. Her essay was memorable for its insight into how classic literature helped her form a distinct identity rooted in intentionality and reflection. Admissions officers were captivated by her mature perspective and her ability to articulate why these seemingly “old-fashioned” values were important in today’s world.
  • The Art of Embracing Complexity: A STEM enthusiast, Nathan was skeptical about studying literature until he encountered The Awakening by Kate Chopin. The ambiguity of the novel’s ending challenged him to rethink his black-and-white view of the world, teaching him that unanswered questions can add value rather than detract from understanding. This newfound appreciation for complexity changed how he approached physics, inspiring him to see the unknown as an opportunity for exploration. Nathan’s essay resonated because it revealed a student willing to be transformed by unexpected experiences. Admissions officers appreciated how Nathan connected his love for science with a new openness to ambiguity, showcasing intellectual curiosity and flexibility.

Celebrating the Unconventional: Essays on Unique Interests and Hobbies

These essays dive into students’ unconventional passions, showing their genuine interests and perspectives. Admissions officers prize students with unique hobbies and passions because they add depth and color to the campus, often bringing a fresh outlook and creative spirit to the academic community.

  • A Love Letter to Hot Sauce: For Sarah, a passion for hot sauce became a symbol of resilience and courage. Her essay traced her journey from a cautious eater to a ghost-pepper enthusiast, drawing an unlikely parallel between handling spice and handling life’s challenges. Through humor and lively storytelling, Sarah celebrated hot sauce as a metaphor for growth, cultural unity, and embracing the unknown. Her essay was successful because it showed how a seemingly trivial passion could reveal character and depth. Admissions officers were drawn to her originality and her ability to see the extraordinary in the ordinary, making her story both memorable and refreshing.
  • The Meditative Art of Quilling: Jacob’s love for quilling, a detailed paper art he learned as a child, became an unlikely foundation for his environmental activism. In his essay, he described how quilling taught him patience, focus, and mindfulness—qualities he later applied when leading a team to advocate for fossil fuel divestment at his school. Jacob’s story was a reminder of how quiet passions can influence larger actions, bridging the gap between the personal and the communal. His essay stood out because it illustrated a sense of dedication that evolved from a hobby into impactful work. Admissions officers admired Jacob’s ability to translate a seemingly simple skill into broader life lessons, showcasing purpose and adaptability.

Conclusion

These essays—each with its own distinctive narrative and voice—showcase the diverse ways students can use storytelling to stand out in the college admissions process. We hope these examples serve as inspiration for students crafting their own unique stories. If you’d like to explore how we guide students through brainstorming and essay writing, reach out to schedule a conversation. Together, we’ll help you bring your story to life!

contentHtml:
At Blue Stars Admissions Consulting, we know that college admissions can feel like a mystery. Parents of high-achieving students often ask: Which activities really matter? How do admissions officers evaluate essays? Do competition awards outweigh leadership roles? Must one play a sport to be considered for elite admissions?

Wonder no more! With our enhanced data-driven advising approach, providing insight backed by real evidence, not guesswork, you will no longer be in the dark. And because Blue Stars has always been deeply analytic in building customized plans for students, this powerful new tool only sharpens our ability to deliver highly personalized, results-rich guidance.

Exclusive Access to the Largest College Admissions Dataset

Through an exclusive partnership, Blue Stars counselors now have access to the largest qualitative admissions dataset in the United States, featuring over 50,000 real student profiles. These anonymized profiles include:

  • Academic statistics and test scores
  • Extracurricular activities and leadership roles
  • Personal essays and authentic narratives
  • Admissions outcomes at top universities

This unprecedented resource offers families a behind-the-scenes look at what truly drives admissions success at the nation’s most competitive schools.

Data + Expertise = Evidence-Based Counseling

Blue Stars has always relied on public databases, institutional reporting, and years of experience to help families cut through the noise. Our new dataset revs that analytic foundation into high gear, giving us real-time insight into what works today—not just what worked five years ago.

How We Use the Data Year by Year

This dataset isn’t just about numbers—it’s about creating a roadmap for students. At Blue Stars, we translate these insights into year-to-year guidance that helps families understand what matters most at each stage of high school. Here’s how we apply the data to shape a student’s journey from 7th grade to senior year:

Why This Matters for Parents

By breaking the process into clear, data-backed steps, families save hours of research and worry. Instead of guessing which activities or courses will have impact, you’ll see the proven patterns of successful applicants—and know how to apply them to your child’s unique path.

author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
For parents of 11th graders aiming for top schools, the stakes couldn’t be higher. Junior year is the time colleges scrutinize most closely, offering your teen a chance to shine academically, focus their passions, and build a compelling application profile. This year presents opportunities to make intentional choices that highlight their unique strengths and future direction.

In this blog post, we’ll guide you through 16 essential steps to help your teen make the most of this crucial year. From achieving high test scores and excelling in rigorous courses to preparing for meaningful summer opportunities and honing time management skills, these strategies will set your teen up for success. 

With your encouragement and a clear plan, junior year can become the launchpad for their college dreams.

16 Things Your 11th-Grader Should Be Doing NOW

1. Ace Junior-Year Classes

The academic transcript is the cornerstone of any college application, often referred to as the “holy grail” of admissions data. Colleges rely on it as the most comprehensive indicator of a student’s academic ability, consistency, and readiness for rigorous coursework. Junior-year grades, in particular, carry the most weight, as they reflect a student’s performance in advanced classes while balancing extracurricular commitments. Help your high school junior prioritize their coursework and seek extra support when needed. Utilize teacher office hours, peer tutoring, study groups, or outside tutoring to stay on top of challenging subjects. If a class becomes too overwhelming, consider switching to an outside accredited program to maintain a strong GPA and safeguard the transcript. Academics must always come first in the college admissions process.

2. Take Rigorous Classes Without Burning Out

Elite colleges value students who challenge themselves with rigorous courses, but balance is essential. Top colleges appreciate applicants who demonstrate sound judgment, steady productivity, and effective time management. They are impressed by students who select challenging coursework while maintaining their mental and physical health. Help your teen choose a course load that is both ambitious and manageable. This allows them to perform well academically while ensuring they can engage meaningfully in other areas like extracurriculars and personal growth.

3. Undertake an In-Depth Project

Top colleges look for students who demonstrate depth and passion in their areas of interest. Independent projects enable students to explore topics deeply, develop problem-solving skills, and showcase initiative. Projects that lead to deliverables or participation in competitions further strengthen a student’s application. Guide your student in undertaking a project aligned with their intended major or interest. Examples include conducting original research, creating a professional portfolio, or launching a community initiative. These efforts highlight critical thinking, project management, and dedication.

4. Volunteer for Impact

By junior year, competitive college applicants will have transitioned from general volunteering to a focused project within a specific area or issue, with measurable deliverables. Admissions officers are impressed by students who make meaningful contributions through sustained, strategic efforts in defined fields. For example, your teen could organize a drive to source free medical equipment for local clinics, manage a tutoring program for underserved students, or lead an environmental campaign to clean up public spaces. These types of projects showcase leadership, initiative, and commitment to a cause.

5. Elevate Leadership in Extracurriculars

By junior year, it’s expected that high school juniors have moved beyond basic participation to advanced leadership roles. Colleges look for applicants who take on significant responsibilities and deliver measurable results. For example, leading a club to raise funds for a meaningful cause or managing a complex team project showcases initiative and impact.

6. Achieve a High Standardized Test Score

Competitive schools often expect standardized test scores in the 1500+ range for the SAT or 34+ for the ACT. Ideally, students will achieve their desired score during the summer before junior year, freeing up time for other priorities. Focused preparation and targeted practice are critical. Help your student create a plan to tackle their weaker areas and register for testing dates early, as spots fill quickly.

7. Prepare for a Competitive PSAT Score

The junior-year PSAT determines eligibility for the National Merit Scholarship, a distinction recognized by many top colleges. Ideally, students will have already completed SAT preparation prior to junior year, as this training provides a solid foundation for the PSAT. Help your teen find support in reviewing the PSAT format and focus on strategies to improve their performance. If your student hasn’t yet started SAT prep, now is the time to create a study schedule and stick to it.

8. Plan a Capstone Junior-Year Summer

Junior-year summer plays a pivotal role in showcasing advanced work related to a student’s academic focus and leadership abilities. Ideally, the experience builds on their 10th-grade summer and reflects their intended plan of study. Support your student in pursuing internships, selective programs, or research opportunities that align with their academic goals. Leadership roles or volunteer efforts tied to their interests can further solidify their admissions narrative.

9. Define a Plan of Study

In our experience, top colleges appreciate high school students who demonstrate a clear academic direction through their selection of a major, double major, or major-minor combination on their applications, rather than choosing “undecided.” The choices students make in high school—academic and extracurricular—serve as evidence of their preparedness for this defined plan. While students may later change their major, initially selecting a specific area of study can significantly strengthen their college applications.

Advise your student to assess the majors offered at their colleges of interest during their junior year to ensure alignment with their high school experiences. If gaps are identified, junior year is a crucial time to engage in activities or courses that enhance their readiness for these desired academic paths. This targeted approach not only clarifies their college intentions but also demonstrates their commitment and readiness for specific college programs.

10. Prep in Advance for AP Tests

AP courses are designed to prepare students for college-level academics, and the AP exams themselves play a key role in demonstrating mastery. It’s beneficial for juniors to allocate additional time for test preparation to achieve top scores. Beginning practice early in the year ensures familiarity with the test format and prevents the stress of last-minute cramming during ‘AP season’ in May. Help your student learn to break preparation into manageable chunks throughout the year. This approach builds confidence and maximizes performance on these important exams.

11. Develop a Balanced School List

Building a thoughtful school list ensures your student has options while aiming for their dream colleges. Work with your teen to categorize schools into Reach, Target, and Safety categories based on academic fit, admissions criteria, and campus culture.Encourage them to research each school’s academic offerings, extracurricular opportunities, and unique programs. This ensures their list reflects both aspiration and practicality.

12. Explore Top-Choice Thoroughly

Colleges appreciate students who show a genuine and well-researched interest in their institution, which can sometimes influence admissions decisions. Ensure your teen attends college fairs, virtual sessions, and campus tours, and most importantly, takes advantage of opportunities to meet college representatives who visit their high school. These interactions provide invaluable insights into a school’s programs, culture, and opportunities while signaling thoughtful engagement. Thorough exploration of top-choice schools not only helps confirm the best fit but also strengthens their application at institutions that track demonstrated interest.

13. Identify Strong Recommendation Writers

Letters of recommendation play a critical role in highlighting your student’s unique qualities and achievements. Work with your teen to identify teachers, mentors, or supervisors who know them well and can write compelling letters. Beyond academic performance, effective letters emphasize leadership, initiative, and character. Help your teen request letters early and provide recommenders with any necessary context or materials to support the writing process.

14. Compete in Relevant Academic Contests and Showcase Achievements 

Support your teen in engaging in contests and opportunities that align with their interests and highlight their subject mastery. STEM students can enter competitions like USACO, AMC, or f=ma, while humanities students might pursue essay contests or publish in peer-reviewed journals. Art students can submit work to Scholastic Art Awards or juried exhibitions. These activities provide tangible evidence of excellence and commitment to their field.

15. Maintain a Polished Resume

A strong resume is essential for college applications, internships, and leadership opportunities. It’s important for your teen to regularly update their resume with awards, extracurricular activities, and leadership roles. This document ideally reflects their accomplishments in a professional, organized format.

16.Refine Communication and Time Management Skills 

Junior year is critical for developing strong communication skills. This is particularly important for writing personal narratives and preparing for interviews. Motivate your student to refine their public speaking and writing abilities. Additionally, effective time management is essential to balance academics, extracurriculars, and application preparation, especially heading into senior year.

Celebrate Success with Us!
As we approach our 15th anniversary in 2025, Blue Stars Admissions Consulting remains dedicated to guiding students toward their dream colleges. With a decade and a half of proven expertise, we know what it takes to succeed. Don’t miss the chance to benefit from our experience and personalized approach. Contact us today to speak with a specialist who can help chart the best course for your teen’s future.

Seize the opportunity with a FREE 30-minute consultation.
Our proven expertise and tailored support have helped families just like yours navigate this critical year with confidence. Let’s work together to make junior year the launchpad for your teen’s bright future!

Don’t wait—spaces fill quickly as we approach application season!

contentHtml:
Strategic Planning. Bold Vision. Brilliant Outcomes.

As has been the case every year during our 15 years of guiding high-achieving students, several Blue Stars students gained admission to the most elite colleges in the country—including Cornell, Brown, and Wellesley—through grit, strategy, and a deep commitment to growth. The 2025 results reflect not just the academic excellence of our students but their drive, preparation, and the powerful outcomes of a thoughtful, individualized admissions strategy.

In an increasingly competitive college landscape, success doesn’t happen by chance. It’s the result of early planning, intentional decisions, and a comprehensive strategy that highlights each student’s authentic story. We are proud to partner with families who trust in the process—and in themselves—to make bold moves toward their futures.

Why Early Decision (ED) Matters

This year, several of our students leveraged Early Decision (ED) to maximize their chances at top-choice schools—and it paid off. ED applicants often face significantly higher acceptance rates than those who apply Regular Decision, but it’s not a decision to be made lightly. title: Meet Blue Stars Counselor Wai Cheng
excerpt: Meet Wai Cheng, a Wharton MBA graduate, who offers expert college admissions counseling, guiding students to top-tier universities like MIT, Stanford, and Yale.

author.name: Wai Cheng
author.bio: Wai Cheng holds an MBA from The Wharton School and advises students on business school, STEM positioning, and top-tier admissions strategy.

contentHtml:
A native New Yorker, Wai brings 10 years of college admissions experience to Blue Stars. Holding a Wharton MBA and Master of International Studies from the University of Pennsylvania and a Bachelor of Art in International Relations from Tufts University, Wai has helped over 100 students majoring in engineering, the natural sciences, social sciences, and humanities reflect upon their stories, discover their strengths, and enter their dream universities like Yale, MIT, Stanford, Johns Hopkins, Amherst, NYU, Tufts, Purdue, and more. He also served on the admissions team for the Wharton Admissions Office in 2021.

Wai began his professional journey at Teach For China, teaching English to 400 rambunctious elementary school students in rural China. Afterward, he joined AIC Education, where he served as an admissions counselor. Influenced by his students, Wai also developed an interest in technology and entertainment.

After graduating from Wharton, Wai joined gaming companies like Electronic Arts as a product manager, working with engineers, art teams, and game designers to provide fun and engaging user experiences. During this time, Wai realized he missed the deep sense of fulfillment he received from mentoring students and helping them grow, leading him to his current role at Blue Stars.

Wai is known for his sense of humor, listening skills, and deep engagement in his students’ advancement, many of whom continue to reach out for advice. Outside of work, Wai volunteers at his church and at a special needs high school in Philadelphia. He loves watching anime and rooting for the New York Knicks, and he is a really bad basketball player.

DrM: With your background in technology and education, how do you help students blend their passion for tech with their college aspirations?

Wai: Whenever I work with students with technology aspirations, I dig into their interests. Why are you interested in STEM? What particular problems are you focused on solving? Who might benefit from your solutions?

Although dreams may change, I find students with larger goals find more success (and meaning) in the application process. They’re not only able to evaluate schools more accurately, but they’re also able to create plans to leverage a school’s resources, preparing them for long-term success.

DrM: How do you use your Wharton experience to guide students who are aiming for top-tier universities?

Wai: Wharton students often struggled with “opportunity paralysis,” an inability to choose resulting from the plethora of opportunities available and desire to do everything.

At Wharton, I overcame opportunity paralysis by defining success on my terms. For example, knowing that I was passionate about technology and also value deep relationships, I embarked on a unique path combining my key interest and core value by joining the Wharton-Lauder International Studies Program, a smaller academic cohort, which led to exciting opportunities in the gaming industry.

This lesson applies to people aiming for top-tier universities. If you find the right program that matches who you are, you set yourself up for success. That’s why I’m passionate about helping my students discover themselves.

DrM: You’ve helped students gain admission to prestigious schools like MIT and Stanford. What do you think makes a student stand out in such a competitive admissions process?

Wai: My MIT and Stanford students had strong academic achievements, often within STEM. However, what made them stand out were special interests that complemented their STEM interests. One was an amazing artist. Another was passionate about anthropology and using documentaries to support their community.

DrM: How does your international experience help you connect with students from diverse  backgrounds and guide them toward success in the college admissions journey?

Wai: When I first traveled to Uganda, I learned the importance of seeking understanding, asking questions and listening. Taking that advice as I’ve traveled the world, I’ve experienced many adventures and met lifelong friends.

Similarly, all our students carry unique stories. As a counselor, my job is to listen and uncover interesting characteristics that students may not see in themselves. The lessons my students learn often shape them deeply, even if they are not initially aware of it.

DrM: What’s the best way for STEM students to showcase their skills and projects in college applications?

Wai: The goal of these achievements is to demonstrate ability and passion.

The fundamental way to showcase ability and passion is excellence in the classroom. Beyond that, students can consider competitions, conducting research, or building their own products. There isn’t one right answer, but whatever you do, pursue excellence, whether entering more challenging competitions, building upon previous research, or iterating on a product for greater impact.

DrM: How do you help students manage the pressures of applying to top schools, especially when they’re juggling challenging STEM projects and academics?

Wai: On a practical level, I communicate with my students to make plans and prioritize. It’s also important to make investments that save time in the long run. For example, brainstorming can be arduous, but if a student brainstorms well, they will expedite the actual writing process.

It’s also important to celebrate victories throughout the process. One of the more special moments I’ve had is seeing a STEM student return and share how he’s applied the lessons he’s learned through the application process to get an A in English.

DrM: What are the most important qualities for a student to develop if they want to succeed in both their college applications and future tech careers?

Wai:
The first trait I think of is grit. I distinctly remember a student who was not a top student in her school. However, she had an extraordinary amount of determination. She applied to over a hundred internships in high school, and although she received many rejections, she eventually landed a dream role helping North Korean refugees. This is the type of student who will continue to overcome challenges in the future.

Another trait is empathy. Our students are our future leaders, and leadership involves being able to understand the needs of diverse stakeholders. If a student is empathetic, they will lead well.

DrM: What’s one piece of advice you wish every high-achieving high school student knew when applying to college?

Wai: Because our students are high achievers, they often feel nervous submitting drafts. When it comes to writing, however, I tell my students that writing is a creative process. Writers, like George R.R. Martin, constantly brainstorm, re-write, and submit their works for review. Students should see themselves as participating in a similar process. The first draft might not be perfect, but through this journey of iterating and revising, we get closer to the final work we’re all proud of. Keep writing, submit work on time, don’t worry about the imperfections, and I promise you, you’ll come out of this a much stronger writer.

title: Demystifying the UC Personal Insight Questions
excerpt: Applying to the University of California (UC) is a unique journey that demands thoughtful reflection and authentic storytelling.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
Unlock Your Full Potential with Our Comprehensive Guide!

Applying to the University of California (UC) is a unique journey that demands thoughtful reflection and authentic storytelling. The UC Personal Insight Questions (PIQs) offer a rare opportunity to showcase your experiences, passions, and personal growth. To help you navigate this critical part of your application, we’ve created a detailed guide filled with expert tips and winning examples.

Why This Guide?

Our expert editors have crafted this guide to provide actionable insights and practical advice. By downloading our comprehensive PDF guide, you’ll gain access to:

  • Unique, successful examples that inspire and guide your writing.
  • Detailed strategies for each PIQ, helping you craft compelling and authentic essays.
  • Bonus introductions and tips to ensure your responses shine.

What’s Inside?

  • Introduction: Six Essential Tips for Acing UC Personal Insight Questions

    Understand the core principles and strategies to make your responses stand out.

  • Question 1: Showcasing Leadership

    Learn how to highlight your leadership experiences and demonstrate your positive influence.

  • Question 2: Creativity

    Discover ways to express your creative side, whether through problem-solving, innovative thinking, or artistic endeavors.

  • Question 3: Writing About Your Greatest Talent or Skill

    Share your journey of developing a particular talent or skill and its impact on your growth.

  • Question 4: Educational Barriers or Opportunities

    Craft compelling narratives about overcoming educational challenges or seizing meaningful opportunities.

  • Question 5: Navigating Challenges and Thriving Academically

    Show how you’ve faced and triumphed over significant challenges in your academic journey.

  • Question 6: Showcasing Your Academic Passion

    Dive deep into your academic interests and illustrate how you’ve pursued them inside and outside the classroom.

  • Question 7: Your Community Impact

    Highlight your contributions to your school or community and demonstrate your problem-solving skills.

  • Question 8: What Makes You Stand Out

    Reflect on your unique qualities and experiences that set you apart as a strong candidate.

Fill out the form now to access this exclusive guide and give your college application the competitive edge it deserves!

excerpt: Join Dr. Amy Morgenstern, founder and CEO of Blue Stars Admissions Consulting, and Jin Chow, Co-founder and COO of Polygence, as they delve into a transformative conversation that challenges long-held beliefs about the earning power of STEM versus humanities majors.

Join Dr. Amy Morgenstern 🧑‍🏫, founder and CEO of Blue Stars Admissions Consulting, and Jin Chow 🤝, Co-founder and COO of Polygence, as they delve into a transformative conversation that challenges long-held beliefs about the earning power of STEM versus humanities majors.

Key Highlights:

Majors and Career Paths: Discover why your chosen major is a poor predictor of your future career and income 💼, with compelling examples from the fields of law and early childhood education.

Earning Power Over Time: Learn about the surprising findings that any earnings advantage STEM majors have over humanities fades by age 40 ⏳, due to the rapid obsolescence of technical skills and the enduring value of humanities-based skills.

Skills That Matter: Understand the critical soft skills employers are looking for—written communication ✍️, problem-solving 🧩, teamwork 👥—and how these are developed through a humanities or liberal arts education.

Real-World Insights: Hear from Jin about how her background in humanities contributed to her success in entrepreneurship, emphasizing the importance of empathy and effective communication 🗣️.

Amy Morgenstern, Ph.D., is the founder of Blue Stars Admissions Consulting 🌠, where personal growth leads to admission to top colleges.

Jin Chow is the driving force at Polygence 🚀, pioneering project-based learning that pairs students with PhD-level mentors for research, career discovery, and passion projects.

title: Pathways to Success: Tips from a Blue Stars Alum and Berkeley Undergrad
excerpt: Meet Evan Davis, a current Berkeley computer science student with a passion for shaping economic policy in the political arena.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
Meet Evan Davis, a current Berkeley student double majoring in Computer Science and Economics. As a member of the Class of 2022 at Laguna Blanca School in Santa Barbara, California, Evan had a passion for shaping economic policy in the political arena. During his senior year, Blue Stars had the pleasure of helping Evan refine his admissions profile.

Highlighting his computer science skills, philosophical interests, and active participation in Junior States of America, we suggested Evan engage in direct political volunteering with Citizens Take Action, an organization focused on reforming campaign finance, further enriching his resume.

In this interview, Evan shares valuable insights for students juggling multiple interests as he has – including adapting when college changes your passions. He also offers tips on making decisions about applying to a variety of colleges, from nationally ranked liberal arts schools to large universities.

We hope you find Evan’s advice and observations as inspiring and insightful as we do!

DrM: How is Berkeley? What is it like to study there, specifically in economics and computer science?

Evan: Berkeley is a hubbub of many different cultures and experiences coming together, teeming with driven and capable people. We have many clubs, research opportunities, and brilliant faculty, but the competition is strong. The academic life here will sweep you away if you’re not careful, so balance is crucial for happiness here.

To be honest, studying economics here was underwhelming for me, because the field’s rich tapestry of multifaceted approaches is largely ignored in favor of only one, and lacks theoretical depth. It’s a better fit for students aiming for industry, policy, or empirical work, not academic theory, as I am. However, Berkeley has amazing faculty and offers some interesting theory-oriented electives.

Computer science is intense. The core courses are designed to be tough, but the electives are amazing. Berkeley offers very theory-oriented computer science classes, including algorithmic economic theory, computability and complexity theory, and courses on AI, machine learning, reinforcement learning, and deep neural networks. For me, this makes up for the economics program’s focus on applied work.

DrM: Are you glad you chose Berkeley?

Evan: Now, yes. Initially, I regretted choosing UC Berkeley over Williams College, preferring Williams’ rural environment. Financial reasons and Berkeley’s stronger CS program influenced my decision. Establishing multiple tight-knit social circles at Berkeley has made me happier with my choice. The theoretical computer science faculty here is also exceptional.

DrM: Has your path changed in ways you didn’t imagine when applying to college?

Evan: Yes. Originally a math and computer science enthusiast, I developed interests in political theory, economics, philosophy, social psychology, and theoretical physics later in high school. I planned then to double-major in Economics and Computer Science with a minor in Philosophy, and have pursued this plan. Discovering my love for academic research, I now intend to pursue a PhD in Economics or Computer Science, applying CS tools to economic theory. I might also pursue a PhD in Machine Learning or Philosophy, depending on how things turn out.

DrM: If there was one myth about college or college admissions you’d like to dispel, what would it be?

Evan: You don’t have to have it all figured out when you start college. College is a time for exploration and fun, as well as career preparation. Many of my friends have switched paths multiple times, and some still don’t know what they want to do. You have time.

DrM: Knowing what you know now, what advice would you give your younger self about gaining admission to a top school?

Evan: Don’t waste the early application season. I should’ve applied early to Brown ED instead of worrying about the one-in-a trillion scenario where getting into Brown would block me from the few schools I preferred at the time (MIT was originally my top choice).

DrM: What do you love about your life?

Evan: I’ve found an amazing social circle at Berkeley and secured strong support from professors for PhD applications (two are co-authoring papers with me). I’m working as a software engineer for a promising startup and have a wonderful social and family life back home. I’m very happy with how things have turned out.

DrM: As you think back to your college planning days, what top three things did you take away from your Blue Stars experience that helped you succeed?

Evan: Don’t be a monolithic STEM kid when you apply to college. Intending to apply technical skills to social causes rather than pure engineering or science can help you get into strong programs, even if you have less technical experience than other applicants. As an example, I got into UCLA’s CS program with almost no CS experience outside of an academic context, when people I know who got rejected had major internship experience and similar grades/coursework.

Combine your passions with unrelated fields (i.e. Chemistry + Philosophy is cooler and more interesting than Politics + Philosophy). This not only strengthens your applications but also enriches your intellectual life. Consider quality of life and your financial situation when choosing a school. Financially, choosing a cheaper school can really help in the long run.

DrM: Any other advice for teens?

Evan: Be assertive and take risks. My few regrets come from not taking action due to fear of rejection. Opportunities I’ve pursued have made my life great. Also, cherish your high school days and memories. Despite the freedom and excitement at college, I sometimes miss the old days and people from high school. I especially cherish my time at Laguna Blanca School.

title: UC Personal Insight Questions: Six Essential Tips for Acing Them
excerpt: In this blog post, we will provide you with six essential tips to help you ace the UC Personal Insight Questions and make a lasting impression on UC admissions officers.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
When it comes to applying to the University of California (UC), the Personal Insight Questions (PIQs) hold significant weight in the admissions process. These questions provide a unique opportunity for you to showcase your experiences, passions, and personal growth.

How can you ensure that your responses stand out from the competition? In this blog post, we will provide you with six essential tips to help you ace the UC Personal Insight Questions and make a lasting impression on UC admissions officers.

1. Understand the Prompt

Before diving into your essay, it is crucial to understand the prompt itself. Take note of key elements and consider how you can structure your response to address each one. By doing so, you will ensure that you are answering the right question and avoid any misinterpretation. It’s best to have the prompt in front of you at all times while working on your essay. By continually referring to the prompt, you will ensure that your response remains aligned with its specific requirements, preventing any deviation that might dilute the impact of your essay.

2. Engage the Senses

To make your essay more captivating and memorable, incorporate sensory details into your narrative. Describe the sights, sounds, and experiences you encountered during the event or project you are discussing. By bringing these sensory elements to life, you will transport the reader into the heart of your story, fostering a deeper connection and engagement.

3. Stay Focused

With a 350-word limit for each UC essay, it is essential to stay focused and avoid the temptation to cover too much ground. Choose one particular aspect of your experience and explore it in depth. By honing in on a specific element, you can provide a more detailed and impactful response that leaves a lasting impression on your readers.

4. Highlight Your Takeaways

Remember that the UC readers are not only interested in the events themselves but also in your reflection and personal growth. Take the time to reflect on the lessons you learned, the insights you gained, and the skills you acquired as a result of your experience. This introspection demonstrates your ability to think critically and extract meaningful conclusions from your encounters.

5. Don’t Get Fancy

While it may be tempting to showcase your writing prowess with elaborate prose and stylistic flourishes, the UC Personal Insight Questions call for a straightforward approach (unlike the Common Application essay prompts). Adopt a conversational tone that reflects your true voice and resembles a personal interview or written account of an experience. Reading your essay out loud can help you ensure that it captures your natural speaking style. If any parts sound unnatural or don’t align with your speaking style, revise those sections accordingly.

6. Draft Multiple Revisions

Writing strong essays often involves multiple drafts. Be prepared to revise your work and explore different ideas before settling on the final version. Don’t be discouraged by initial rough drafts; even the best writers go through this process. Patience and perseverance will lead to a more polished and impactful essay.

Crafting compelling UC Personal Insight Question responses requires careful thought, reflection, and revision. But above all, remember the importance of remaining authentic and true to yourself throughout the application process.

Admissions officers are not necessarily impressed by a perfectly crafted essay. They want to get to know the real you, the person behind the application. By staying true to yourself, you will not only create a more compelling and impactful essay but also increase your chances of standing out among the sea of applicants.

Your story is valuable and deserves to be shared. With these five essential tips and your authentic voice guiding you, you are well-equipped to ace the UC Personal Insight Questions and make a lasting impression. Good luck, and may your essays truly reflect the remarkable individual that you are!

title: Is It Advantageous to Answer Personal Insight Question 8?
excerpt: Personal Insight Question 8 demands deep introspection, creativity, and a delicate balance between showcasing your unique qualities and character without coming across as boastful.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
“Beyond what has already been shared in your application, what do you believe makes you stand out as a strong candidate for admission to the University of California?”

Personal Insight Question 8 demands deep introspection, creativity, and a delicate balance between showcasing your unique qualities and character without coming across as boastful.

In this blog post, we’ll guide you through a thoughtful response to PIQ 8, offering insight on whether answering this question will work to your advantage or not.

Before you start, it’s important to think about what it means to “stand out.”

Personal Insight Question 8 can initially feel perplexing and even intimidating, as it challenges you to differentiate yourself from other applicants. Often, it can lead either to self-doubt or, on the other side of the spectrum, the temptation to brag about achievements.

In responding to this question, we encourage you to think beyond conventional notions of success. Consider what sets you apart in terms of your character, experiences, and values. Avoid the temptation to compare yourself to others.

Here are eight tips to guide you in crafting a compelling response to PIQ 8:

1. Think Deeply, Critically, and Creatively

Take time to reflect deeply on your life experiences, challenges, and personal growth. Consider moments that have shaped you and values that are dear to your heart. Think creatively about how these aspects define your uniqueness.

2. Check for Suitability

Ask yourself whether the idea you’ve come up with for this essay is genuinely the best fit for it. If it feels more appropriate for a different essay prompt, consider using it there instead.

3. Avoid Repetition

Ensure that the content of your essay doesn’t duplicate information already present in your application. This essay should offer new insights into your character and experiences.

4. Find a Humble Tone

Resist the urge to boast or exaggerate your accomplishments. Instead, convey your strengths with humility and authenticity.

5. Connect Content to Character

Bridge the gap between the experiences or qualities you share and your character. How have these experiences shaped your values and principles? How do they reflect who you are as a person?

6. Emphasize Your Character as a Strong Candidate

Highlight how your unique qualities and experiences make you a strong candidate for UC admissions. Draw a clear connection between your individuality and your potential to contribute positively to the campus community.

7. Ensure Complementarity

Ensure that your response complements and reinforces the other essays in your application. Your essays should collectively provide a well-rounded view of your character and experiences.

8. Don’t Feel Obligated

Remember that you don’t have to answer this question to stand out in the admissions pool. While it’s an opportunity to showcase your uniqueness, it’s just one aspect of your application. Don’t let the pressure of this question overwhelm you.

Remember, your response to PIQ 8 should not only make you stand out but also offer insights into your character, values, and the qualities that make you a strong candidate for UC admissions. Approach this essay with thoughtfulness, creativity, and a genuine desire to share your unique perspective with the admissions committee. By doing so, you’ll craft a standout application that reflects the true essence of who you are.

In this blog post, we'll guide you through a thoughtful response to PIQ 8, offering insight on whether answering this question will work to your advantage or not. Before you start, it’s important to think about what it means to “stand out.” Personal Insight Question 8 can initially feel perplexing and even intimidating, as it challenges you to differentiate yourself from other applicants. Often, it can lead either to self-doubt or, on the other side of the spectrum, the temptation to brag about achievements. In responding to this question, we encourage you to think beyond conventional notions of success. Consider what sets you apart in terms of your character, experiences, and values. Avoid the temptation to compare yourself to others. Here are eight tips to guide you in crafting a compelling response to PIQ 8: 1. Think Deeply, Critically, and Creatively Take time to reflect deeply on your life experiences, challenges, and personal growth. Consider moments that have shaped you and values that are dear to your heart. Think creatively about how these aspects define your uniqueness. 2. Check for Suitability Ask yourself whether the idea you've come up with for this essay is genuinely the best fit for it. If it feels more appropriate for a different essay prompt, consider using it there instead. 3. Avoid Repetition Ensure that the content of your essay doesn't duplicate information already present in your application. This essay should offer new insights into your character and experiences. 4. Find a Humble Tone Resist the urge to boast or exaggerate your accomplishments. Instead, convey your strengths with humility and authenticity. 5. Connect Content to Character Bridge the gap between the experiences or qualities you share and your character. How have these experiences shaped your values and principles? How do they reflect who you are as a person? 6. Emphasize Your Character as a Strong Candidate Highlight how your unique qualities and experiences make you a strong candidate for UC admissions. Draw a clear connection between your individuality and your potential to contribute positively to the campus community. 7. Ensure Complementarity Ensure that your response complements and reinforces the other essays in your application. Your essays should collectively provide a well-rounded view of your character and experiences. 8. Don't Feel Obligated Remember that you don't have to answer this question to stand out in the admissions pool. While it's an opportunity to showcase your uniqueness, it's just one aspect of your application. Don't let the pressure of this question overwhelm you. Remember, your response to PIQ 8 should not only make you stand out but also offer insights into your character, values, and the qualities that make you a strong candidate for UC admissions. Approach this essay with thoughtfulness, creativity, and a genuine desire to share your unique perspective with the admissions committee. excerpt: What is it like to live in ultra-aspirational Palo Alto, gain experience as a Stanford University admissions officer, work privately with ultra-ambitious students seeking admission to elite colleges, and mother three children who don't fit into the idealized Silicon Valley model of high-achievement?

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
What is it like to live in ultra-aspirational Palo Alto, gain experience as a Stanford University admissions officer, work privately with ultra-ambitious students seeking admission to elite colleges, and mother three children who don’t fit into the idealized Silicon Valley model of high-achievement? You can find out in this informative, lively interview with Dr. Irena Smith about her book, The Golden Ticket: A Life in College Admissions Essays.

In this intimate, astute, and wide-ranging memoir, Dr. Irena Smith shares her journey of setting up the perfect life in one of the most coveted suburbs in America and learning that the universe had other lessons for her – lessons she hadn’t necessarily asked for but perhaps needed, like what it means to truly honor your child’s uniqueness. She also imparts her insight on how we can create more authentic relationships with our kids.

We talk a little bit about Stanford admissions, too! And there’s the section connecting Dr. Smith’s work to Malcom Harris’s Palo Alto: A History of California, Capitalism, and The World. It was a pleasure speaking with my friend and colleague, Dr. Irena Smith, during this in-depth interview. I hope you enjoy it!

title: 10 Things Your 8th Grader Should Be Doing Now for Top College Admissions
excerpt: By following these critical steps, your child will not only become a strong applicant but also develop essential skills and values for success in college and life.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
It might seem surprising to start this early, but with the increasing competition and evolving expectations of college admissions, 8th grade is not too soon to begin preparing. If you want your child to grow in ways that impress top schools, it’s crucial to lay the groundwork now.

By following these critical steps, your child will not only become a strong applicant but also develop essential skills and values for success in college and life. Early preparation ensures they are ready to tackle the challenges ahead, positioning them favorably for admissions success.

1. Address Fundamental Skill Gaps in Math

If your child struggles with math, now is the time to address these challenges. Remedial tutoring or summer programs can help strengthen these foundational skills. Even for students interested in the humanities, solid quantitative skills pave the way to an Ivy League or other top-tier school.

2. Plan an Accelerated Math Track

For students interested in engineering and other STEM fields, plan their high school math trajectory early. Investigate whether they need to take placement tests or summer courses to advance into higher-level classes like Linear Algebra or Multivariable Calculus later on in high school. This is particularly important if your child is aiming for a STEM career. Successful top school applicants often present experience in math well beyond the typical high school curriculum.

3. Enhance Essay Writing Skills

Teens who have difficulty expressing themselves in writing will fall behind in high school and lose momentum in gaining entry to a top tier school like Stanford, Harvard, or UC Berkeley. Enrolling in a summer writing course can help your child hone this essential skill, preventing it from becoming a bottleneck later.

4. Develop Organizational and Time Management Skills

If your student tends to procrastinate or struggles with organizing assignments, summer is the perfect time to focus on these crucial skills. Tools and courses that enhance time management and organization can be invaluable. When evaluating applications, top school admissions officers will note how well each applicant manages their time as a factor in their decision-making. A student who has done little beyond school work, or students who spread themselves too thin with many superficial commitments will not be viewed as favorably as those who prioritized commitments and executed specific plans with results.

5. Learn to Code

In today’s tech-driven world, coding is a fundamental skill, especially for those interested in STEM fields, but also for humanities students. A humanities student who knows code (but is not necessarily a wizard) will be invaluable for collaborative teams bridging diverse skill sets. Summer offers a low-pressure opportunity to learn programming without the stress of grades affecting college applications. Top schools appreciate humanities students who go beyond their comfort zone, or humanities students who excel in both the humanities and coding.

6. Read Regularly

Continual reading is essential for intellectual growth. The more parents can guide their child in reading both nonfiction and fiction, the more they will stand out in admissions and succeed in life. We encourage introducing “device-free” time on a regular basis to create quiet conditions for the kind of sustained concentration needed for a good, deep read. It could make all the difference in your child’s path.

7. Explore Interests Through Clubs and Volunteering

Getting involved in clubs, sports, music, or volunteering helps students discover their passions and build a well-rounded profile. These activities are critical for personal development and appealing college applications. Be advised that helping a younger teen find volunteer opportunities can be challenging because of age restrictions. This means that extra effort and creative problem-solving might be needed to get your child on the right track. If you want your child to be considered for admission at a top school, this early effort will be worth it! We also often encourage parents to volunteer with their child at this early stage for an easier introduction to volunteering and parent-child bonding.

8.Establish Healthy Routines and Digital Literacy

Learning how to unplug from devices, engage in real-life interactions, and reserve time for deep concentration will instill a personal strength and integrity in your child. Emphasize good social media habits and digital literacy, and establish a balanced routine for health, exercise, sleep, and stress management. Encourage setting limitations on screen time to ensure your child has time for offline activities and meaningful interactions. Rituals and routines help tremendously in this regard. A person in control of their attention, not ceding it to distractions, will be noticed by top school admissions officers.

9. Cultivate Effective Study and Note-Taking Habits

Developing strong study habits and note-taking strategies early is crucial for academic success. Help your child establish a routine, encourage critical thinking while writing, and use visual elements to enhance notes. Minimize distractions to improve focus. Explore the highest-rated, age-specific note-taking applications with your child. Investigate different note-taking methods, such as the Cornell system or outlining, to find what works best for them.

10. Develop a Sense of Global and Community Awareness

Top colleges seek students who are engaged with their communities and the world, beyond just academic excellence. Encourage your 8th grader to care about issues, volunteer, and start thinking globally. For example, they could organize a neighborhood cleanup to promote environmental awareness or start a school recycling program. Volunteering at local shelters or participating in community gardens are also great ways for them to get involved and develop a sense of responsibility.

By focusing on these areas, you can help your 8th grader build a strong foundation for significantly boosting their chances of gaining admission to top colleges. Early preparation not only positions your child as a strong applicant but also instills in them the skills and values necessary for success in college and life.

We are committed to helping your child reach their full potential and achieve their academic goals.

title: Students Admitted to 29 Prestigious Summer Courses
excerpt: We are thrilled to announce that our 9th-11th graders have been accepted into 29 selective summer courses this year.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
COSMOS, New York Times, Canada/USA Math Camp, Wharton, and More!

We are thrilled to announce that our 9th-11th graders have been accepted into 29 selective summer courses this year. These programs span multiple disciplines, from humanities to science and technology, offering our students incredible opportunities for academic enrichment and personal growth.

Attending a summer program offers high school students – particularly those aiming for top colleges – numerous admissions advantages:

  • Academic Enrichment: Summer programs provide advanced coursework and hands-on experience in various fields, enabling students to deepen their knowledge and skills beyond the high school curriculum. Top colleges are impressed by students who study beyond what is offered in their high school classes and demonstrate a commitment to academic excellence and intellectual curiosity.

  • Research Opportunities: Working directly with university professors in specialized summer courses demonstrates a student’s dedication and passion for their field. Elite colleges value this proactive approach, as it showcases a readiness for advanced study.

  • Networking Opportunities: Students meet peers with similar interests and ambitions, as well as professionals and academics in their field, building valuable connections that can benefit their admissions chances and future careers.

  • College Preparation: These programs often simulate college environments, helping students adjust to college-level academics and campus life, which can ease the transition from high school to university.

  • Personal Growth: Beyond academics, summer programs help students develop independence, confidence, and critical thinking skills, preparing them for the challenges of higher education and beyond.

Programs like those listed below might be considered an investment in your child’s future, ensuring they are well-prepared for the rigors of top-tier universities and the challenges of the professional world.

We are incredibly proud of our students’ achievements and look forward to seeing the remarkable contributions they will make in their respective fields. Congratulations to all who have been accepted into these impressive programs!

The Blue Stars Advantage

Our expert counselors conduct rigorous research to help students choose the exact programs that match each student’s specific interests or set of interests, help them craft winning application essays starting with brainstorming, and partner with them on submitting a perfect application.

Find out more about our exhaustive database of hundreds of summer opportunities!

In addition to summer programs, Blue Stars has secured exclusive relationships with vendors offering unique internship and research opportunities. These opportunities give students unparalleled access to real-world experiences that enhance their academic and professional profiles.

Click here for a free, 30-minute consultation to find out more about our customized summer planning!

Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM)

Program Description
Canada/USA Math Camp Offers a rigorous mathematical curriculum designed for talented high school students, fostering a deep understanding of mathematical concepts and problem-solving skills.
COSMOS UCLA Cluster 4: High Success: Hydrogen Is Green Headway to SUstainability, Carbon Capture, Energy-transition, and SUStainizability® Focuses on sustainable technologies and practices, including hydrogen energy, carbon capture, and energy transition, offering students a chance to engage in cutting-edge scientific research.
COSMOS UCLA Cluster 1: Brain-Inspired Computing: Learning in Biological; Artificial Neural Networks Explores the fascinating field of brain-inspired computing, combining biological insights with artificial neural network research to advance students’ understanding of computational neuroscience.
COSMOS UC Davis Cluster 3: Introduction to Engineering Mechanics Introduces students to the principles of engineering mechanics, providing a strong foundation in the analysis and design of mechanical systems.
Harvard Ventures-TECH Summer Program (HVTSP) Offers students a chance to work directly with venture-backed startups, learning about entrepreneurship and polishing their technical and business skills through exclusive seminars with founders, venture capitalists, and Harvard faculty.
Michigan Math and Science Scholars (MMSS) Offers talented high school students a rich and challenging environment to explore advanced topics in mathematics and science through field-specific, focused seminars, lectures, and labs led by University of Michigan faculty.
UChicago Summer Immersion Pathways in Data Science Provides a comprehensive introduction to data science through interactive lectures and hands-on projects. Students learn to analyze and interpret complex datasets, using tools and techniques essential for data-driven decision-making to create a final project.
UCLA Engineering Design Summer Institute Immerses students in the field of mechanical engineering, providing hands-on experience in design, prototyping, and problem-solving.
UCSC Science Internship Program (SIP) – Research Group CSE-02: Building Intelligent Android Agents to Complete Tasks With Instruction Guidance Work directly with UC Santa Cruz professors on cutting-edge research on artificial intelligence, focusing on developing intelligent android agents for task completion.
Wharton Data Science Academy Introduces students to the fundamentals of data science with a focus on business applications, combining theory with practical exercises. Students work with data sets to solve actual business problems using statistical and machine learning techniques.
Northwestern College Preparation Program Focus Seminars: Time, Space & the Future Quantum Mechanics and Relativity Delves into advanced topics in physics, including quantum mechanics and relativity, offering students a deeper understanding of these fundamental concepts.
UCSD Academic Connections: Ocean Ecosystems Explore marine biology and oceanography, gaining hands-on experience in the study of ocean ecosystems and marine life.
UCSB Research Mentorship Program (RMP) Pairs high school students with university researchers to conduct original research, providing invaluable experience in scientific inquiry and academic writing.

Business and Economics

Program Description
Berkeley Business Academy for Youth (BBAY) Introduces high school students to the fundamentals of business, including finance, marketing, and entrepreneurship, through creating a business plan and pitching it to a panel of judges.
Wharton Leadership in the Business World Prepares students for leadership roles in business, focusing on developing essential skills such as strategic thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork through lectures, workshops, and hands-on projects.
Wharton SF-Based Innovation and Start-Ups Immerses students in the start-up culture, teaching them about innovation, product development, and entrepreneurial strategies through creating a business plan for an original business.

Medicine and Health Sciences

Program Description
BU AIM: Introduction to Experimental Psychology Offers a deep dive into experimental psychology, providing hands-on research experience and exposure to advanced concepts in psychology.
Springboard Emergency Medicine Program Provides students with an introduction to emergency medicine, including clinical skills, patient care, and medical simulations.
Stanford SASI Foundations and Clinical Skills Programs Through two separate programs, the Stanford Anesthesia Summer Institute (SASI) provides students with hands-on experience in clinical skills, foundational medical knowledge, and design thinking, offering insights into the field of medicine.
Summer@Brown Medicine in Action: A View Into the Life of a Medical Student Provides an inside look at medical school, offering students hands-on experience in medical simulations, patient care, and clinical skills.
UChicago Summer Immersion – Developmental Psychology Explores developmental psychology, offering students hands-on research experience and exposure to advanced concepts in the field.
UCSD School of Medicine Research Scholars: Sports Medicine Summer Academy Focuses on sports medicine, offering students practical experience in injury prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation.

Humanities and Social Sciences

Program Description
The Concord Review History Camp Supports high-achieving students in learning the skills to produce outstanding original research papers.
Democracy Summer Engages students in political and civic education and direct campaign experience, promoting active citizenship.
Northwestern College Preparation Program Focus Seminars: Abnormal Psychology – Analyzing Life with Mental Illness Offers high school students a deep dive into abnormal psychology, focusing on understanding mental illnesses and their impacts on daily life. Participants study psychological disorders, their diagnoses and treatments, using case studies and current research.
The School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC) Early College Program Summer Institute Enables high school students to take college-level fine arts, design, and creative writing courses at one of the nation’s leading art schools.
School of the New York Times Summer Camp Learn about reporting, writing, and multimedia storytelling through workshops and real-world exploration under the guidance of reporters and editors from The New York Times.
UChicago Summer Immersion Economics from an Experimental Perspective Offers students an opportunity to delve into economics through experimental methods. Participants engage in hands-on activities and experiments to understand economic theories, behavioral economics, and the impact of decision-making processes on economic outcomes.
Yale Young Global Scholars: Literature, Philosophy, and Culture Track A unique opportunity to explore the intersections of literature, philosophy, and cultural studies through a diverse curriculum and interactive discussions.

title: Exploring the True Value of Humanities and STEM Majors in Career Success
excerpt: Join Dr. Amy Morgenstern, founder and CEO of Blue Stars Admissions Consulting, and Jin Chow, Co-founder and COO of Polygence, as they delve into a transformative conversation that challenges long-held beliefs about the earning power of STEM versus humanities majors.

author.name: Dr. Amy Morgenstern
author.bio: Dr. Amy Morgenstern ('Dr. M') founded Blue Stars in 2010. She holds a Ph.D. and MFA, and created 'The Calm Way' methodology to guide students to Ivy League and top-choice acceptances.

contentHtml:
In our latest video discussion, Dr. Amy Morgenstern, founder and CEO of Blue Stars Admissions Consulting, joins Jin Chow, Co-founder and COO of Polygence, to debunk common myths about the career and income prospects associated with STEM and humanities majors.

Insightful Highlights Include:

  • Majors and Career Paths: Often, we hear that choosing a major directly correlates with future earnings and career trajectory. However, this conversation sheds light on why this isn’t necessarily true.
  • Earning Power Over Time: It might surprise you to learn that the earning advantage seen in STEM fields can diminish by the age of 40. This shift occurs as quickly evolving technical skills can become obsolete, whereas the skills cultivated through a humanities education remain highly valuable and applicable across various industries.
  • Skills That Matter: Jin and Dr. Morgenstern discuss essential soft skills—like communication, problem-solving, and teamwork—that employers truly value and how these are often honed in a humanities-focused education.
  • Real-World Insights: Jin Chow shares how her humanities background was instrumental in her success as an entrepreneur, highlighting critical skills such as empathy and effective communication.

Why This Matters for You:

Whether you are preparing for college or planning your career, understanding these dynamics can significantly influence your educational and professional decisions. Blue Stars Admissions Consulting is dedicated to guiding students through the college admissions process with a focus on long-term career success, regardless of their major.

Watch and Learn

We invite you to watch the full discussion on our website and gain a deeper understanding of how your educational choices can impact your career. This enlightening conversation offers valuable perspectives whether you are drawn to the humanities or STEM fields.

Reach Out for Expert Guidance

Embark on your educational journey with confidence. Visit Blue Stars Admissions Consulting and Polygence for personalized advice on college and career planning. Let us help you unlock your full potential.

Find Out More

For a deeper dive into the value of humanities versus STEM majors, we hope you read Jin Chow’s article in Forbes. With her unique background in comparative literature and expertise in multiple languages, Jin offers a compelling perspective on the critical importance of humanistic skills in today’s education landscape.
